title: Array Random Access by Address Arithmetic
subject: Data Structures
statement: An array stores equal-sized elements contiguously, so the i-th element is located by one address computation in worst-case O(1) time.
short: Contiguous storage turns indexing into a single arithmetic step.
long: Contiguous storage turns indexing into a single arithmetic step. Random access is the defining strength of arrays; insertion or deletion in the middle costs O(n) because elements must shift.
proof: The address of a_i is base + i times element size, which is computed and dereferenced in constant time on a RAM.
consequence: Arrays are the default representation when indexed reads dominate and the size is stable.

title: Dynamic Array Amortised Append
subject: Data Structures
statement: Doubling the capacity whenever a dynamic array is full gives amortised O(1) time per append.
short: Occasional expensive resizes are paid for by many cheap appends.
long: Occasional expensive resizes are paid for by many cheap appends. Copying n elements at the n-th resize can be charged to the O(n) appends since the previous doubling, giving total O(n) for any n appends.
proof: Aggregate method: total copies over n appends are at most n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n, so total work is O(n).
consequence: Dynamic arrays combine constant-time indexing with effectively constant-time growth, as in C++ vector or Python list.

title: Shrink Hysteresis in Dynamic Arrays
subject: Data Structures
statement: A growing array that shrinks at one-quarter occupancy and grows at full occupancy avoids resize thrashing.
short: Separated thresholds prevent alternating insert/delete from resizing every step.
long: Separated thresholds prevent alternating insert/delete from resizing every step. After shrinking from half-full at quarter-full, at least n/2 more insertions are needed before another growth, so the amortised bound survives.
proof: Each resize requires Omega(n) operations since the previous one; charging each operation a constant amortised cost covers both kinds of resize.
consequence: Practical hash tables and vectors use such hysteresis to keep memory proportional to size without instability.

title: Linked List Insertion at a Known Node
subject: Data Structures
statement: Given a pointer to a node, insertion after it in a singly linked list takes O(1) time by rewiring two next pointers.
short: Pointer rewiring beats shifting when the position is already known.
long: Pointer rewiring beats shifting when the position is already known. Finding the position by traversal still costs O(i); the O(1) bound applies only when the predecessor pointer is in hand.
proof: Only the new node's next field and the predecessor's next field change, a constant number of assignments.
consequence: Linked lists excel when many edits occur at already-known positions and sequential traversal is acceptable.

title: Linked List Search Is Linear
subject: Data Structures
statement: Searching a singly linked list for a value takes O(n) worst-case time because nodes are scattered in memory and only sequential access is available.
short: Without contiguous storage there is no index to jump to.
long: Without contiguous storage there is no index to jump to. Even if the list is sorted, binary search does not apply because locating the midpoint requires traversal.
proof: After inspecting k nodes the only known boundary is the k-th node, so an adversary can place the target at the end.
consequence: Linked structures trade random access for cheap splicing, which is why they appear in queues and adjacency-like chain structures.

title: Doubly Linked List Deletion
subject: Data Structures
statement: A node in a doubly linked list can be deleted in O(1) time given its pointer, by updating both neighbours.
short: Backward links make unlinking a node constant-time.
long: Backward links make unlinking a node constant-time. A singly linked list needs the predecessor, which generally requires a traversal unless the deletion is by swapping successor data.
proof: The two neighbour pointers are available at the node, so four assignments detach it.
consequence: Doubly linked lists underpin LRU caches and free lists where arbitrary nodes must be removed quickly.

title: Sentinel Nodes Eliminate List Edge Cases
subject: Data Structures
statement: A dummy sentinel head and tail node let list code treat empty and boundary cases like ordinary nodes.
short: Sentinels move special cases out of the main loop.
long: Sentinels move special cases out of the main loop. Circular sentinels also make splice and concatenate operations uniform, at the cost of one or two extra nodes.
proof: Every real node has both a predecessor and a successor once sentinels are present, so no null checks are needed in the loop body.
consequence: This pattern appears in kernel lists, skip lists and balanced-tree implementations to simplify invariants.

title: Stack Last-In First-Out Discipline
subject: Data Structures
statement: A stack supports push and pop at one end, returning elements in reverse order of insertion (LIFO).
short: The most recently added item is the next one removed.
long: The most recently added item is the next one removed. Array-backed stacks give O(1) amortised push and O(1) pop; linked stacks give O(1) worst-case for both.
proof: Only the top pointer or index changes on each operation, so all operations are constant-time.
consequence: Stacks implement expression evaluation, recursion simulation, backtracking and depth-first traversal.

title: Queue First-In First-Out Discipline
subject: Data Structures
statement: A queue inserts at the rear and removes at the front, preserving arrival order (FIFO).
short: The oldest waiting item is served next.
long: The oldest waiting item is served next. A circular buffer avoids shifting elements, giving O(1) amortised operations with fixed capacity.
proof: Two pointers (front and rear) advance modulo the array size, so each operation is constant-time.
consequence: Queues are the core of breadth-first search, buffers, schedulers and message-passing systems.

title: Deque Supports Both Ends
subject: Data Structures
statement: A double-ended queue supports insertion and deletion at both front and rear in amortised O(1) time.
short: A deque generalises both stacks and queues.
long: A deque generalises both stacks and queues. A circular array or a doubly linked list implements it; Python collections.deque uses a block-based circular structure.
proof: End operations adjust only boundary pointers, with occasional amortised resizing of a circular array.
consequence: Deques support sliding-window algorithms and work-stealing schedulers efficiently.

title: Monotonic Stack for Next Greater Element
subject: Data Structures
statement: A stack that keeps decreasing values computes the next greater element for every position in O(n) total time.
short: Each index is pushed and popped once.
long: Each index is pushed and popped once. Pop smaller elements when a larger one arrives, assigning them the current index as their answer, then push the current index.
proof: Every index enters and leaves the stack at most once, so the total number of stack operations is O(n).
consequence: The same pattern solves histogram largest rectangle and daily-temperature style problems.

title: Sliding Window Maximum with a Deque
subject: Data Structures
statement: Maintaining candidate indices in a decreasing deque answers all sliding-window maxima in O(n) time.
short: The deque is a queue of candidates ordered by value.
long: The deque is a queue of candidates ordered by value. Drop expired indices from the front and remove dominated smaller values from the back before inserting the new element.
proof: Each index is inserted once and removed once, so total work is linear.
consequence: It gives an optimal streaming solution for fixed-window range maxima.

title: Binary Heap Shape and Order Invariant
subject: Data Structures
statement: A binary heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is at most (min-heap) or at least (max-heap) its children.
short: Complete shape plus a parent-child order yields an array-friendly priority queue.
long: Complete shape plus a parent-child order yields an array-friendly priority queue. Completeness means the tree can be stored in an array with children of index i at 2i and 2i+1, with no pointers needed.
proof: The invariants are exactly the conditions required for extract-min to restore order by sift-down along one root-to-leaf path.
consequence: Heaps provide compact, cache-friendly priority queues for Dijkstra's algorithm and heapsort.

title: Heap Insert and Extract-Min
subject: Data Structures
statement: Insertion sifts a new element up and extract-min sifts the replacement down, both in O(log n) worst-case time.
short: Repairing one root-to-leaf path costs logarithmic time.
long: Repairing one root-to-leaf path costs logarithmic time. Sift-up swaps with the parent while the order is violated; sift-down swaps with the smaller child.
proof: A binary heap of n nodes has height floor(log2 n), and each sift moves along one path.
consequence: Heaps implement priority queues with a logarithmic worst-case bound per update.

title: Bottom-Up Heapify Is Linear
subject: Data Structures
statement: Building a heap from n arbitrary keys by sifting down all internal nodes bottom-up takes O(n) time, not O(n log n).
short: Most nodes are near the leaves, where sift-down is short.
long: Most nodes are near the leaves, where sift-down is short. Repeated insertion would cost O(n log n); bottom-up construction exploits the shape of complete trees.
proof: At height h there are at most n/2^{h+1} nodes and each costs O(h); summing n h/2^h over h gives O(n).
consequence: Heapsort's build phase is linear, so its total O(n log n) bound comes entirely from extraction steps.

title: Heap Order Does Not Imply Sorted Order
subject: Data Structures
statement: In a min-heap the array [1, 5, 2, 9, 7] satisfies the heap property but is not sorted.
short: Heap order is only between parent and children, not between siblings.
long: Heap order is only between parent and children, not between siblings. A heap guarantees only that the minimum is at the root; siblings and subtrees have no relative ordering.
proof: Check 1 <= 5,2 and 5 <= 9,7; nevertheless 5 > 2, so the array is not sorted.
consequence: Heap traversal alone cannot produce sorted output; heapsort must repeatedly extract the minimum.

title: d-ary Heap Time Trade-off
subject: Data Structures
statement: In a d-ary heap, height is O(log_d n) and extract-min costs O(d log_d n), so moderate d can reduce total cost.
short: More children make the tree shallower but each sift-down compares more children.
long: More children make the tree shallower but each sift-down compares more children. Insertion remains O(log_d n); the best d depends on the insert-to-delete-min ratio and memory behaviour.
proof: A complete d-ary tree of n nodes has height log_d n, and sift-down examines d children per level.
consequence: Four-ary heaps are common in practice because they reduce height while keeping comparisons cheap.

title: Hash Table with Separate Chaining
subject: Data Structures
statement: Separate chaining stores each bucket as a list of all keys hashing to it, so collisions are resolved locally.
short: Colliding keys share a bucket list.
long: Colliding keys share a bucket list. With m buckets and n keys the load factor is alpha = n/m; search cost is 1 + expected chain length.
proof: Insertion links a new node into the bucket, and search scans exactly that bucket.
consequence: Chaining degrades gracefully when the table is full and supports arbitrary key types with a hash function.

title: Open Addressing and Linear Probing
subject: Data Structures
statement: Linear probing resolves collisions by scanning successive slots cyclically until an empty slot is found.
short: All data lives in the table, with probe sequences handling collisions.
long: All data lives in the table, with probe sequences handling collisions. Successful and unsuccessful searches take expected O(1/(1-alpha)) probes at load factor alpha < 1; clustering can make constant factors large.
proof: Under uniform hashing the expected probe count is the geometric sum over the free fraction of the table.
consequence: Open addressing saves pointers and improves cache locality, but requires careful deletion via tombstones.

title: Simple Uniform Hashing Expected Chain Length
subject: Data Structures
statement: Under simple uniform hashing, the expected number of keys in any chain is the load factor alpha = n/m.
short: Uniform hashing spreads keys evenly on average.
long: Uniform hashing spreads keys evenly on average. An unsuccessful or successful search therefore takes expected Theta(1 + alpha) time.
proof: Each of n keys lands in a fixed bucket with probability 1/m, so by linearity of expectation the expected count is n/m.
consequence: Keeping the load factor bounded gives expected constant-time dictionary operations.

title: Universal Hashing Against Adversarial Keys
subject: Data Structures
statement: Choosing a hash function at random from a universal family bounds the expected collision count for any fixed set of n keys by n(n-1)/(2m).
short: Randomising the function removes the adversary's ability to force collisions.
long: Randomising the function removes the adversary's ability to force collisions. Universality means any two distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/m under a randomly chosen function.
proof: Linearity of expectation over the n choose 2 pairs gives the bound independent of the input distribution.
consequence: Universal hashing restores expected O(1) performance even when keys are chosen after the algorithm is fixed.

title: FKS Perfect Hashing
subject: Data Structures
statement: Two-level perfect hashing stores a static set of n keys in O(n) space with O(1) worst-case lookups.
short: A second hash table per bucket eliminates all collisions.
long: A second hash table per bucket eliminates all collisions. The top level uses a universal hash function; each bucket of size k gets its own table of size k^2, which has O(n) total expected size.
proof: Universality bounds the probability of a collision in a size-k^2 secondary table by 1/2, so expected total space is linear.
consequence: Perfect hashing is the standard solution for static dictionaries with strict lookup-time guarantees.

title: Cuckoo Hashing Constant-Time Lookup
subject: Data Structures
statement: Cuckoo hashing uses two hash functions and two tables so every key resides in one of two slots, giving O(1) worst-case lookup.
short: Two candidate slots per key make searching constant-time.
long: Two candidate slots per key make searching constant-time. Insertion may evict and relocate occupants; if a cycle occurs the tables are rehashed, which is expected O(1) amortised at constant load.
proof: Only two fixed slots need inspection on a lookup; insertion terminates with constant probability per step below the load threshold.
consequence: It is used in high-performance caches and routers where worst-case lookup latency matters.

title: Hash Tables Do Not Preserve Key Order
subject: Data Structures
statement: A hash table gives no ordering of keys, so range queries and ordered iteration require a different structure.
short: Hashing scrambles key order by design.
long: Hashing scrambles key order by design. Even with a monotone-looking hash function, collisions and bucket placement destroy a total order; use a tree or sorted array instead.
proof: A hash function maps keys to bucket indices based on arithmetic that is not order-preserving in general.
consequence: Dictionaries and sets are hash-based; maps needing predecessor or range queries use balanced trees.

title: Binary Search Tree Inorder Ordering
subject: Data Structures
statement: In a binary search tree every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger than the node's key, so inorder traversal yields sorted order.
short: The local ordering rule gives a globally sorted traversal.
long: The local ordering rule gives a globally sorted traversal. Search, insert and delete follow one root-to-leaf path, costing O(h) time where h is the height.
proof: Induction on tree size: inorder visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, each recursively sorted.
consequence: BSTs support ordered dictionary operations if balance is controlled.

title: BST Cost Is Governed by Height
subject: Data Structures
statement: All basic BST operations take O(h) worst-case time, where h ranges from log2 n to n-1.
short: Balance, not node count alone, determines BST speed.
long: Balance, not node count alone, determines BST speed. A balanced tree has logarithmic height; a path-shaped tree degenerates to linear search time.
proof: Each operation descends at most one level per visited node, following a single branch at each step.
consequence: Self-balancing schemes exist precisely to keep h logarithmic.

title: Sorted Insertion Degenerates a BST
subject: Data Structures
statement: Inserting keys 1,2,3,...,n into an ordinary BST in increasing order creates a chain of height n-1.
short: Without rebalancing, sorted input is worst-case input.
long: Without rebalancing, sorted input is worst-case input. Searching for the last inserted key then costs n comparisons, not log2 n.
proof: Each new key exceeds all previous ones, so it is always attached as the right child of the previous maximum.
consequence: Unbalanced BSTs are unsafe for adversarial or naturally sorted streams; use AVL, red-black or randomised trees.

title: AVL Height Balance Invariant
subject: Data Structures
statement: An AVL tree requires the heights of a node's two subtrees to differ by at most one, which forces height O(log n).
short: Local height balance implies global logarithmic height.
long: Local height balance implies global logarithmic height. The minimum number of nodes N(h) in an AVL tree of height h satisfies N(h)=1+N(h-1)+N(h-2), a Fibonacci-like recurrence.
proof: Solving the recurrence gives N(h) >= phi^h, hence h = O(log n).
consequence: AVL trees guarantee O(log n) worst-case search, insertion and deletion with tight height.

title: AVL Rotations Restore Balance
subject: Data Structures
statement: After an AVL insertion, at most a double rotation at the first unbalanced ancestor restores the invariant; deletion may need O(log n) rotations.
short: Local pointer flips repair height balance.
long: Local pointer flips repair height balance. The four cases are left-left, right-right, left-right and right-left, the latter two resolved by two rotations.
proof: Insertion changes heights along one path; a single or double rotation at the lowest unbalanced node restores its previous height.
consequence: AVL updates remain O(log n) even though rebalancing is required.

title: Red-Black Tree Colour Invariants
subject: Data Structures
statement: A red-black tree colours nodes so that every path from a node to its leaves has the same number of black nodes and no red node has a red child.
short: Equal black-heights keep all root-to-leaf paths comparable.
long: Equal black-heights keep all root-to-leaf paths comparable. The root is black and nil leaves are treated as black; these rules allow heights up to twice the optimal.
proof: The equal black-height rule forces each root-to-leaf path to have at least half its nodes black.
consequence: Red-black trees give O(log n) worst-case dictionary operations with cheaper updates than AVL trees.

title: Red-Black Height Logarithmic Bound
subject: Data Structures
statement: A red-black tree with n internal nodes has height at most 2 log2(n+1).
short: Equal black-height plus no adjacent reds caps the depth.
long: Equal black-height plus no adjacent reds caps the depth. The bound is looser than AVL's but still guarantees logarithmic worst-case operations.
proof: Removing red nodes leaves a tree in which every root-to-leaf path has equal length and at least n+1 leaves, giving black-height at least log2(n+1); every path has at most twice that many nodes.
consequence: The bound justifies red-black trees as the default self-balancing tree in standard libraries.

title: Splay Tree Amortised Access
subject: Data Structures
statement: A splay tree moves each accessed node to the root with rotations and achieves O(log n) amortised time per access.
short: Recently used keys migrate toward the root.
long: Recently used keys migrate toward the root. Individual operations can cost O(n), so the guarantee is amortised; no explicit balance fields are stored.
proof: The potential is the sum of logarithmic subtree sizes; sifting a node up decreases this potential enough to pay for rotations.
consequence: Splay trees exploit temporal locality and are simple, with strong guarantees such as the static optimality property.

title: Treap Randomised Balance
subject: Data Structures
statement: A treap stores keys in BST order and independent random priorities in heap order, giving expected O(log n) height.
short: Random priorities make a balanced shape likely.
long: Random priorities make a balanced shape likely. Insertion rotates a new node up while its priority beats its parent's; deletion rotates it down and removes it.
proof: Priorities induce a uniformly random permutation of nodes, and the expected depth of a node in a random BST is O(log n).
consequence: Treaps are simple randomised balanced trees used in ordered maps and randomised persistent structures.

title: B-Tree Height in Disk Blocks
subject: Data Structures
statement: A B-tree of minimum degree t has height O(log_t n), so each search touches O(log_t n) nodes.
short: High fan-out compresses the tree to few disk pages.
long: High fan-out compresses the tree to few disk pages. Every node except the root has between t-1 and 2t-1 keys, so the number of leaves grows exponentially with height.
proof: A tree of height h has at least 2t^{h-1} leaves, giving h <= 1 + log_t(n/2).
consequence: B-trees minimise block transfers, which is why databases index with them.

title: B+ Tree Keeps Records at Leaves
subject: Data Structures
statement: A B+ tree stores records only in linked leaves and keeps keys in internal nodes purely as routing separators.
short: Separating index from records makes range queries cheap.
long: Separating index from records makes range queries cheap. Internal nodes can hold more routing keys, and leaf links allow sequential scans without tree traversal.
proof: All records are at the same depth and leaf siblings are chained, so a range scan follows successor links.
consequence: B+ trees are the dominant index structure in relational databases and filesystems.

title: Trie for Prefix Queries
subject: Data Structures
statement: A trie stores strings as paths from a root, with each edge labelled by a symbol, so all keys sharing a prefix share a path.
short: Common prefixes are stored only once.
long: Common prefixes are stored only once. Lookup, insertion and deletion take O(|s|) time independent of the number of stored strings; space can be large for sparse nodes.
proof: Following the symbols of s traverses exactly one edge per symbol.
consequence: Tries support autocomplete, IP routing tables and dictionary spell-checking.

title: Radix Tree Compresses Trie Paths
subject: Data Structures
statement: A radix (Patricia) tree compresses each maximal chain of single-child trie nodes into one edge labelled by a string.
short: Unary paths collapse into labelled edges.
long: Unary paths collapse into labelled edges. Space becomes proportional to the number of keys rather than total key length in many cases, while lookup stays O(|s|).
proof: Each compressed edge represents a path that had only one child and thus no branching decision.
consequence: Radix trees back many routers and key-value stores, including compressed tries for integer keys.

title: Disjoint-Set Union-Find ADT
subject: Data Structures
statement: Union-find maintains a partition of elements with make-set, find and union operations.
short: It tracks which elements belong to the same component.
long: It tracks which elements belong to the same component. A forest of parent pointers represents sets; the root is the representative.
proof: Following parent pointers from any node reaches the root, which identifies the set.
consequence: Union-find is the backbone of Kruskal's algorithm, connected-component labelling and many offline algorithms.

title: Union by Rank with Path Compression
subject: Data Structures
statement: Attaching the shorter tree to the taller one and compressing find paths yields almost constant-time union-find operations.
short: Short trees plus flattened paths keep depth tiny.
long: Short trees plus flattened paths keep depth tiny. Path compression rewires visited nodes directly to the root; union by rank bounds tree height before compression.
proof: Rank only increases along compressed paths, and the classic analysis bounds total work by the inverse Ackermann function.
consequence: Essentially all connected-component computations run in near-linear time.

title: Inverse Ackermann Bound for Union-Find
subject: Data Structures
statement: A sequence of m union and find operations on n elements with union by rank and path compression takes O((m+n) alpha(n)) time, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function.
short: The bound grows more slowly than any practical iterated logarithm.
long: The bound grows more slowly than any practical iterated logarithm. For any conceivable n the inverse Ackermann function is at most four or five, so the bound is effectively linear.
proof: Tarjan's potential argument charges path traversals to rank increases, with the Ackermann hierarchy controlling the sum.
consequence: It is one of the sharpest amortised results in algorithm analysis.

title: Skip List Expected Logarithmic Search
subject: Data Structures
statement: A skip list layers sorted linked lists with geometrically random tower heights, giving expected O(log n) search, insert and delete.
short: Random express lanes make linked-list search logarithmic.
long: Random express lanes make linked-list search logarithmic. Worst-case search is O(n) because tower heights are random, not enforced.
proof: The height of each node is geometric with parameter p, so backward analysis of the search path gives expected logarithmic length.
consequence: Skip lists offer a simple randomised alternative to balanced trees, used in Redis sorted sets and leveldb-like stores.

title: Bloom Filter Has No False Negatives
subject: Data Structures
statement: A Bloom filter uses k hash functions to set k bits per inserted key; a query may report a false positive but never a false negative.
short: Deleted or absent keys can slip through, present keys never do.
long: Deleted or absent keys can slip through, present keys never do. If any queried bit is zero the key is definitely absent; if all are one it is probably present.
proof: Inserting a key sets all its bits, so a present key always finds them set unless bits were incorrectly cleared.
consequence: Bloom filters cheaply avoid expensive disk or network lookups for absent keys.

title: Bloom Filter False Positive Rate
subject: Data Structures
statement: For m bits, n inserted keys and k hash functions, the false positive probability is approximately (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k, minimised at k = (m/n) ln 2.
short: More hash functions help until bits saturate.
long: More hash functions help until bits saturate. The optimal k balances false positives from too few probes against bit saturation from too many.
proof: A given bit stays zero with probability (1 - 1/m)^{kn} ≈ e^{-kn/m}; independence gives the k-th power.
consequence: Sizing a filter from n and a target p is a standard engineering calculation in large-scale systems.

title: Counting Bloom Filter Supports Deletion
subject: Data Structures
statement: Replacing bits by small counters allows deletions at the cost of extra space and possible counter overflow.
short: Counters undo the bit settings of a removed key.
long: Counters undo the bit settings of a removed key. Each insertion increments k counters and deletion decrements them; false positives still occur.
proof: Decrementing exactly the counters set at insertion restores the state as if the key were never added, barring collisions.
consequence: Counting filters support dynamic sets in routers and caches, though counter sizing needs care.

title: Bitvector Rank and Select Operations
subject: Data Structures
statement: A succinct bitvector supports rank_1(i) (number of ones up to i) and select_1(j) (position of the j-th one) in O(1) time with o(n) extra bits.
short: Succinct structures compress data while keeping random access.
long: Succinct structures compress data while keeping random access. Blocks with superblock counters and small lookup tables trade a little redundancy for constant-time queries.
proof: Precomputed counts per block reduce a query to a table lookup plus a short local scan.
consequence: Rank/select is the building block of succinct trees, bitmaps and compressed text indexes.

title: Sparse Table for Static Range Minimum
subject: Data Structures
statement: A sparse table answers static range-minimum queries in O(1) time after O(n log n) preprocessing, using O(n log n) space.
short: Overlapping power-of-two blocks let two intervals cover any range.
long: Overlapping power-of-two blocks let two intervals cover any range. It requires a static array; updates invalidate the precomputed minima.
proof: A range of length L is covered by two precomputed blocks of length 2^{floor(log L)}, whose minimum is the answer for idempotent operations like min.
consequence: Sparse tables are the simplest constant-time RMQ solution for read-only data.

title: Cartesian Tree from an Array
subject: Data Structures
statement: The Cartesian tree of an array is the binary tree with heap-ordered priorities given by array values and inorder order given by indices.
short: Heap order from values, inorder from positions.
long: Heap order from values, inorder from positions. It can be built in linear time with a monotonic stack and is equivalent to the LCA structure used in RMQ.
proof: Scanning left to right, stack the rightmost spine and attach each new element after popping larger priorities.
consequence: Cartesian trees connect RMQ to lowest-common-ancestor queries and describe treap shapes.

title: Leftist Heap Merge in Logarithmic Time
subject: Data Structures
statement: A leftist heap merges two heaps in O(log n) worst-case time by recursively merging the right spines.
short: A null-path-length invariant keeps the merge path short.
long: A null-path-length invariant keeps the merge path short. Each node stores its null path length, and swapping children when needed keeps the right spine logarithmic.
proof: The null path length of a leftist tree is at most log2(n+1), bounding the recursive merge path.
consequence: Leftist heaps give meldable priority queues with a clean worst-case guarantee.

title: Skew Heap Amortised Merge
subject: Data Structures
statement: A skew heap merges by swapping children at every node on the merge path unconditionally, giving O(log n) amortised merge.
short: Aggressive swapping keeps the structure balanced in aggregate.
long: Aggressive swapping keeps the structure balanced in aggregate. It needs no balance fields, unlike leftist heaps, but has no per-operation worst-case bound.
proof: Potential based on the number of heavy children pays for the swaps along the merge path.
consequence: Skew heaps are simple meldable heaps with good practical performance.

title: Binomial Heap Structure
subject: Data Structures
statement: A binomial heap is a collection of binomial trees obeying heap order, with at most one tree of each rank.
short: Binary representation of n controls the heap's shape.
long: Binary representation of n controls the heap's shape. Meld is like binary addition; insert, meld and extract-min take O(log n) worst-case time.
proof: The ranks present correspond to the 1-bits of the element count, so at most log2 n trees exist.
consequence: Binomial heaps support efficient meld and were a precursor to Fibonacci heaps.

title: Fibonacci Heap Amortised Decrease-Key
subject: Data Structures
statement: A Fibonacci heap supports insert, meld and decrease-key in O(1) amortised time and extract-min in O(log n) amortised time.
short: Lazy restructuring postpones work until a delete-min forces consolidation.
long: Lazy restructuring postpones work until a delete-min forces consolidation. Decrease-key cuts a node and may cascade cuts up the tree; the potential stored in marked nodes pays for them.
proof: The potential is the number of trees plus twice the number of marked nodes; consolidation and cascading cuts are charged against it.
consequence: It improves Dijkstra and Prim on dense graphs to O(E + V log V) amortised.

title: Pairing Heap Practical Performance
subject: Data Structures
statement: Pairing heaps are simple multiary meldable heaps that perform very well in practice despite lacking a tight amortised proof for all operations.
short: Elegant in code, resisted exact analysis for years.
long: Elegant in code, resisted exact analysis for years. Meld is a pointer comparison and extract-min merges children in two passes; known upper bounds are close to but not exactly O(log n).
proof: Meld of two heaps simply compares roots and attaches the smaller under the larger, a constant-time operation.
consequence: They are a common pragmatic choice when meldable heaps are needed and worst-case bounds are not critical.

title: van Emde Boas Tree for Small Universes
subject: Data Structures
statement: A van Emde Boas tree supports predecessor, successor, insert and delete on a universe of size u in O(log log u) time.
short: Recursive sqrt-sized summaries give doubly logarithmic depth.
long: Recursive sqrt-sized summaries give doubly logarithmic depth. It uses O(u) space and is fastest when the key universe is modest, such as machine words or small integers.
proof: Splitting the universe into sqrt(u) clusters and recursing on a summary gives T(u)=T(sqrt u)+O(1), hence log log u.
consequence: It breaks the log n comparison barrier for integer keys by exploiting the bounded universe.

title: Y-Fast Trie Reduces vEB Space
subject: Data Structures
statement: A y-fast trie stores n keys from a u-element universe in O(n) space with expected O(log log u) predecessor searches.
short: Buckets of balanced trees mimic a vEB tree with linear space.
long: Buckets of balanced trees mimic a vEB tree with linear space. Each bucket holds O(log u) keys in a balanced tree; a hash table maps bucket representatives.
proof: A vEB tree on the O(n/log u) bucket representatives plus local tree search gives the stated bound.
consequence: It gives near-vEB speed with linear storage, important for large integer universes.

title: Binary Trie for Integer Keys
subject: Data Structures
statement: A binary trie on fixed-width integer keys branches on successive bits, supporting insert, lookup and predecessor in O(w) time for word size w.
short: Bit-level branching gives a bounded-depth tree.
long: Bit-level branching gives a bounded-depth tree. With 32- or 64-bit keys the depth is a machine constant, making tries competitive with hashing.
proof: Each key has exactly w bits, so any search traverses at most w levels.
consequence: Binary tries underlie IP longest-prefix matching and compressed integer indexes.

title: Interval Tree for Overlap Queries
subject: Data Structures
statement: An interval tree stores intervals in a balanced tree keyed by left endpoint with augmented maximum right endpoints, reporting all overlaps in O(log n + k) time.
short: Augmented maxima prune branches that cannot overlap.
long: Augmented maxima prune branches that cannot overlap. The max-right field at each node tells whether any interval in a subtree can intersect the query.
proof: Search both children only when their maximum right endpoint exceeds the query's left endpoint, charging visited nodes to output or path length.
consequence: Interval trees are used in calendar scheduling, computational geometry and compiler register allocation.

title: Quadtree Hierarchical Space Partition
subject: Data Structures
statement: A quadtree recursively subdivides two-dimensional space into four quadrants, storing points or occupancy in the leaves.
short: Spatial subdivision makes region queries local.
long: Spatial subdivision makes region queries local. Point quadtrees split at points, region quadtrees split at geometric midlines; depth depends on point distribution.
proof: Each subdivision reduces the region size by half, so a point is stored at depth proportional to its coordinate precision.
consequence: Quadtrees support spatial indexing, image compression and collision detection.

title: k-d Tree Average-Case Nearest Neighbour
subject: Data Structures
statement: A k-d tree recursively splits points by alternating coordinate axes, giving O(log n) expected nearest-neighbour search for well-distributed points and O(n) worst case.
short: Axis-aligned splits prune most of space on typical data.
long: Axis-aligned splits prune most of space on typical data. Range queries in two dimensions take O(sqrt(n)+k) expected time for balanced random data.
proof: A balanced split halves the point set each level, so the query follows one branch with occasional backtracking.
consequence: k-d trees are a simple baseline for low-dimensional nearest-neighbour search, though curse of dimensionality hurts high dimensions.

title: Priority Queue as an Abstract Data Type
subject: Data Structures
statement: A priority queue supports insert and extract-min (or extract-max) on items with comparable keys, independent of any particular implementation.
short: Order by priority, not by arrival time.
long: Order by priority, not by arrival time. Common implementations are binary heaps (O(log n) worst case), Fibonacci heaps (amortised improvements) and balanced trees.
proof: The ADT is specified by its operations and their effect on the multiset of keys, not by storage details.
consequence: It is the key abstraction behind Dijkstra, Prim, Huffman coding and event-driven simulation.

title: Heap versus Balanced Tree for Priority Queues
subject: Data Structures
statement: A heap is smaller and faster for pure priority-queue operations, while a balanced tree supports ordered queries such as predecessor and range scan.
short: Choose by which operations you need, not by asymptotic equality.
long: Choose by which operations you need, not by asymptotic equality. Heaps lack efficient arbitrary delete or search by key; trees pay extra pointer and rotation overhead.
proof: Both maintain logarithmic height, but trees additionally preserve a total key order across all nodes.
consequence: Dijkstra typically uses a heap; an ordered set of active keys requires a tree.

title: Move-to-Front Self-Organising List
subject: Data Structures
statement: Move-to-front moves a requested item to the head of an unstructured list, giving competitive performance on sequences with locality.
short: Temporal locality is exploited without knowing access probabilities.
long: Temporal locality is exploited without knowing access probabilities. Its competitive ratio against the optimal static ordering is at most 2, and it matches the optimal offline cost up to a constant factor.
proof: An element pays at most one extra move per other element moved ahead of it, giving constant competitiveness via a potential argument.
consequence: The idea appears in caching heuristics and entropy coding transforms.

title: LRU Cache with Hash Map and Doubly Linked List
subject: Data Structures
statement: A hash map to nodes plus a doubly linked list in recency order supports get and put in O(1) expected time.
short: Hashing finds the node, list order tracks recency.
long: Hashing finds the node, list order tracks recency. On access the node is spliced to the front; on overflow the tail is evicted.
proof: Map lookups are expected constant and list splicing uses stored predecessor/successor pointers.
consequence: This is the canonical implementation of least-recently-used caches in operating systems and databases.

title: Persistent Stack by Node Sharing
subject: Data Structures
statement: A persistent stack allocates a new head node on push and shares the unchanged tail, so old versions remain accessible in O(1) time and space per update.
short: Immutable nodes let versions share structure.
long: Immutable nodes let versions share structure. Persistence can be partial (only newest version updated) or full (all versions updated); here updates return a new stack.
proof: A new node points to the old head, so both versions are valid linked lists with no mutation of shared nodes.
consequence: Persistent structures underpin functional programming, undo mechanisms and versioned indexes.

title: CSR Compressed Sparse Matrix Format
subject: Data Structures
statement: Compressed sparse row stores nonzero values, their column indices and row-start offsets in three arrays.
short: Only nonzeros are stored, with row boundaries recorded.
long: Only nonzeros are stored, with row boundaries recorded. Matrix-vector multiplication takes O(nnz) time; random element access is slower than in dense format.
proof: Row pointers delimit contiguous slices of values and column indices for each row.
consequence: CSR is the standard sparse-matrix format in scientific computing and graph algorithms.

title: Adjacency List versus Adjacency Matrix
subject: Data Structures
statement: Adjacency lists use O(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours in O(deg v), while adjacency matrices use O(V^2) space and test edge existence in O(1).
short: Sparse graphs favour lists; dense graphs favour matrices.
long: Sparse graphs favour lists; dense graphs favour matrices. Traversal with a matrix costs O(V^2) even for sparse graphs, while repeated edge queries favour matrices.
proof: Lists store each edge once, matrices store one bit per ordered pair.
consequence: Choosing the representation often dominates the practical cost of graph algorithms.

title: Structure of Arrays Improves Cache Use
subject: Data Structures
statement: Storing each field in a separate contiguous array can speed up kernels that access only one field, compared with an array of records.
short: Fetch only the bytes the kernel actually reads.
long: Fetch only the bytes the kernel actually reads. It improves spatial locality and enables vectorisation, but hurts when all fields of a record are needed together.
proof: Cache lines then contain only useful field values rather than interleaved unused bytes.
consequence: SoA layout is common in high-performance graphics, physics and columnar databases.

title: Linked Structure Memory Locality Penalty
subject: Data Structures
statement: Pointer-based structures can be asymptotically optimal yet slower than arrays because each node may cause a cache miss.
latex: O(1)\ pointers,\ O(1)\ cache\ miss\ each
short: Big-O hides the cost of chasing pointers through memory.
long: Big-O hides the cost of chasing pointers through memory. A pointer-rich tree or list scatters allocations, while an array-backed heap or open-addressed table prefetches well.
proof: Each node dereference may map to a different cache line, and cache misses dominate arithmetic on modern hardware.
consequence: Cache-aware design sometimes prefers arrays and implicit indices over elegant pointer structures.

title: Amortised Cost of Repeated Minimum Extraction
subject: Data Structures
statement: Repeatedly extracting the minimum from a heap built once costs O(n log n) total, since the build is linear and each of n extractions costs O(log n).
short: Build once, then pay only for the extractions.
long: Build once, then pay only for the extractions. This is the exact cost profile of heapsort's selection phase.
proof: Linearity of the build plus the heap height bound on each extraction gives the total.
consequence: It explains why heapsort matches merge sort asymptotically without extra space.

title: Union-Find in Online Connected Components
subject: Data Structures
statement: Processing edges in any order and unioning endpoints maintains connected components of an undirected graph incrementally.
short: Union-find answers connectivity as edges arrive.
long: Union-find answers connectivity as edges arrive. It cannot handle deletions, which require dynamic connectivity structures.
proof: The equivalence relation generated by processed edges is exactly connectivity in the graph of those edges.
consequence: This is the standard fast path for Kruskal's algorithm and percolation simulations.

title: Try-and-Error Search Versus Dictionary Lookup
subject: Data Structures
statement: Searching among n items by checking membership in a hash table takes expected O(1) per probe, but finding an unknown key still requires n probes in the worst case.
short: Fast membership does not replace a search problem.
long: Fast membership does not replace a search problem. A hash table answers 'is x present?' instantly but cannot list nearby keys or discover a target without a candidate.
proof: Without order or a candidate-generation rule, at least one probe per possible key may be needed.
consequence: Dictionaries accelerate verification, not discovery; ordered indexes are needed for range search.

title: Comparison Sorting Lower Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case to sort n distinct items.
short: There are n! possible orders and each comparison is binary.
long: There are n! possible orders and each comparison is binary. The bound holds regardless of implementation tricks, but non-comparison sorts can beat it for restricted key types.
proof: A decision tree with n! leaves has depth at least log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) by Stirling's formula.
consequence: Merge sort, heapsort and introsort are asymptotically optimal comparison sorts.

title: Decision Tree Model for Sorting
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: In the decision tree model each internal node is a comparison between two keys, each branch is an outcome, and each leaf is a permutation.
short: Sorting is a game of twenty questions over permutations.
long: Sorting is a game of twenty questions over permutations. The model ignores arithmetic on keys, which is precisely why it does not apply to counting or radix sort.
proof: Every possible input ordering must reach a distinct leaf, so the tree must have at least n! leaves.
consequence: This model supplies the standard optimality proof for comparison sorts.

title: Insertion Sort and Its Costs
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right; it is O(n^2) worst and average case, O(n) best case, uses O(1) extra space and is stable.
short: Simple, stable and fast on small or nearly sorted arrays.
long: Simple, stable and fast on small or nearly sorted arrays. It is often used as the base case for quicker recursive sorts.
proof: Shifting costs O(i) for the i-th element, summing to O(n^2); equal keys are never swapped past each other.
consequence: Its stability and low overhead make it the standard small-subarray routine in hybrid sorts.

title: Insertion Sort Adaptive Bound by Inversions
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Insertion sort runs in Theta(n + I) time where I is the number of inversions in the input.
short: Nearly sorted inputs with few inversions finish almost linearly.
long: Nearly sorted inputs with few inversions finish almost linearly. This is a precise adaptivity measure: an already sorted array has I = 0 and costs linear time.
proof: Each shift removes exactly one inversion, and each element requires at least one comparison.
consequence: It explains why insertion sort outperforms asymptotically better algorithms on small perturbations.

title: Selection Sort Trade-off
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted suffix and swaps it into place, taking Theta(n^2) time and O(1) space.
short: Minimal writes, quadratic comparisons.
long: Minimal writes, quadratic comparisons. The straightforward version is not stable because a swap can move an equal element past another.
proof: Finding the minimum of a suffix of size k costs k-1 comparisons, giving n(n-1)/2 comparisons in total.
consequence: It is useful when writes are expensive, but dominated on speed by insertion or heap sort.

title: Bubble Sort with Early Exit
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; with a swapped flag it takes O(n) on sorted input and O(n^2) otherwise, is stable and uses O(1) space.
short: Adjacent swaps bubble large elements to the end.
long: Adjacent swaps bubble large elements to the end. Its educational value exceeds its practical value, though it is simple for tiny inputs.
proof: Each pass places at least one element in final position, and adjacent equal keys are not swapped.
consequence: It illustrates stability and best-case analysis in a minimal setting.

title: Merge Sort Recurrence and Stability
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts recursively and merges, giving Theta(n log n) time, O(n) extra space and stable output.
short: Divide, conquer, then linearly interleave.
long: Divide, conquer, then linearly interleave. It has the same bound on all inputs, unlike quicksort, and the merge step preserves the relative order of equal keys.
proof: The recurrence solves to Theta(n log n); taking from the left run first on ties keeps sorting stable.
consequence: Merge sort is the textbook optimal comparison sort and the basis of external and parallel sorting.

title: Bottom-Up Merge Sort Without Recursion
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Starting with runs of length 1, repeatedly merge adjacent runs of equal length until one run remains, in Theta(n log n) time.
short: Iterative doubling replaces the recursion stack.
long: Iterative doubling replaces the recursion stack. It uses alternating source and destination arrays to avoid copying at every level.
proof: After k passes all runs have length 2^k, so log2 n passes suffice, each costing O(n).
consequence: It is convenient in iterative environments and forms the skeleton of tape merge sort.

title: Stable In-Place Merge Is Harder
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Merging two sorted adjacent runs stably in O(1) extra space is possible but requires sophisticated rotation-based algorithms with O(n) time.
short: Constant-space stable merging needs careful block movements.
long: Constant-space stable merging needs careful block movements. Naive in-place merging shifts elements and can degrade to O(n^2); practical sorts accept O(n) auxiliary space.
proof: Symmetric and rotation-based merges move blocks of smaller elements left while preserving order, charging moves to elements relocated.
consequence: Space-constrained stable sorting is a classic algorithmic engineering problem.

title: Quicksort Partition Step
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Quicksort chooses a pivot, partitions elements into those below and above it, then sorts the two sides recursively.
short: A linear partition splits the problem into two smaller ones.
long: A linear partition splits the problem into two smaller ones. Partitioning is in-place but not stable; the cost depends heavily on how balanced the split is.
proof: Each partition scans the current subarray once, and recursion terminates when a subarray has at most one element.
consequence: Its cache-friendly in-place behaviour makes quicksort the default general-purpose sort in many libraries.

title: Quicksort Expected Linearithmic Time
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: With random pivots or randomly ordered input, quicksort runs in expected O(n log n) time with O(log n) expected stack depth.
short: Random splits give a logarithmic expected recursion depth.
long: Random splits give a logarithmic expected recursion depth. The worst case remains O(n^2), so randomisation is essential for unpredictable inputs.
proof: Each pair of elements is compared with probability at most 2/(j-i+1), and summing these probabilities gives 2n ln n.
consequence: Randomised quicksort is fast in practice and has a clean average-case guarantee.

title: Quicksort Worst Case on Sorted Input
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Always choosing the first element as pivot makes quicksort take Theta(n^2) time on already sorted or reverse-sorted input.
short: A consistently bad pivot creates a depth-n recursion.
long: A consistently bad pivot creates a depth-n recursion. The partition is maximally unbalanced, leaving subproblems of sizes 0 and n-1.
proof: Summing the partition costs n + (n-1) + ... + 1 gives n(n+1)/2 comparisons.
consequence: Pivot selection is not a minor detail; production quicksorts randomise or use median-of-three.

title: Randomised Pivot Guarantees Expected Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Selecting the pivot uniformly at random at every recursive call yields expected O(n log n) time for every fixed input.
short: Randomness removes dependence on input order.
long: Randomness removes dependence on input order. The bound is expected over the algorithm's random choices, not a worst-case guarantee.
proof: The expected recurrence satisfies E[T(n)] <= (2/n) sum E[T(k)] + O(n), solved by substitution.
consequence: Randomisation is a standard tool for eliminating pathological inputs.

title: Three-Way Partition Quicksort
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Partitioning into less-than, equal-to and greater-than regions makes quicksort linear when the input has few distinct keys.
short: Duplicates are handled once instead of recursively.
long: Duplicates are handled once instead of recursively. Dutch national flag partitioning groups all pivot-equal elements in one pass.
proof: If there are d distinct keys, at most d partitions occur at each level with total linear work per level, and d is constant here.
consequence: Three-way partitioning is crucial for sorting data with many repeated values.

title: Introsort Worst-Case Guarantee
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Introsort starts as quicksort but switches to heapsort when recursion depth exceeds twice log2 n, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case.
short: A safety valve stops quicksort's bad case before it happens.
long: A safety valve stops quicksort's bad case before it happens. It also uses insertion sort for small subarrays, as in the standard C++ std::sort.
proof: Depth-limited quicksort spends O(n log n) before switching; heapsort finishes any remaining subarray in O(n log n).
consequence: It combines quicksort's speed with a hard worst-case bound.

title: Heapsort and Its Guarantees
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Heapsort builds a max-heap then repeatedly swaps the root with the last element and sifts down, giving Theta(n log n) worst-case time, O(1) space and an unstable order.
short: In-place sorting via a priority queue.
long: In-place sorting via a priority queue. Its worst case matches its average case, unlike quicksort, but it has poorer cache locality.
proof: Linear heapify plus n extract-max operations each costing O(log n) gives the bound; swaps of distant elements destroy stability.
consequence: Heapsort is preferred when memory is tight and worst-case time must be bounded.

title: Counting Sort for Bounded Integer Keys
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Counting sort tallies occurrences of each key in a range 0..k and reconstructs the output in O(n+k) time.
short: When keys are small integers, counting beats comparison.
long: When keys are small integers, counting beats comparison. It is stable if prefix sums are used, and space is O(n+k); it is impractical when k greatly exceeds n.
proof: One pass counts keys, a prefix-sum pass computes starting positions, and a stable pass places each element.
consequence: It is the final digit sort in radix sort and useful for small-range integer data.

title: Prefix Sums Make Counting Sort Stable
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Replacing counts by prefix sums gives the starting output position for each key, so scanning the input left to right preserves equal-key order.
short: Running totals tell each key where to go.
long: Running totals tell each key where to go. Decrementing the start pointer after each placement fills each key's block from left to right.
proof: All elements with smaller keys occupy earlier positions, and equal keys are placed in encounter order.
consequence: Stability of counting sort is what makes LSD radix sort correct.

title: LSD Radix Sort Complexity
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Least-significant-digit radix sort processes d digits with base b in O(d(n+b)) time using a stable sort per digit.
short: Sort by each digit in turn, from right to left.
long: Sort by each digit in turn, from right to left. It is not comparison-based, so it can beat Omega(n log n) when digits are small and d is bounded.
proof: Each of d passes is a counting sort on b buckets costing O(n+b); stability preserves earlier digit order.
consequence: Radix sort is fast for fixed-width integers and strings with short keys.

title: MSD Radix Sort and Recursion
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Most-significant-digit radix sort partitions by the leading digit and recurses on each bucket, sorting variable-length keys naturally.
short: Left-to-right digit recursion handles strings.
long: Left-to-right digit recursion handles strings. It can switch to insertion sort once buckets are small, and needs care with differing key lengths.
proof: Grouping by the first digit places all keys in the correct final block; recursion orders keys within each block.
consequence: MSD radix is the basis of several fast string-sorting routines.

title: Radix Sort Needs Stable Digit Passes
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: LSD radix sort is correct only if every digit pass is stable; an unstable pass destroys the ordering by less significant digits.
short: Later passes must preserve earlier decisions.
long: Later passes must preserve earlier decisions. MSD radix sort does not require stability across buckets because each bucket is processed independently.
proof: If two keys agree on the current digit, their relative order must be whatever the lower digits established.
consequence: This is a classic example where a seemingly minor property of a subroutine is essential.

title: Bucket Sort Expected Linear Time
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: If n keys are drawn independently and uniformly from [0,1), distributing them into n buckets and sorting each by insertion sort takes expected O(n) time.
short: Uniform inputs spread evenly over buckets.
long: Uniform inputs spread evenly over buckets. The worst case is O(n^2) when all keys land in one bucket; widening the number of buckets reduces this risk.
proof: The expected number of keys per bucket is constant, and the sum of squared bucket sizes is O(n) in expectation.
consequence: Bucket sort illustrates how distribution assumptions can break the comparison lower bound.

title: Shell Sort Gap Sequence Dependence
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Shell sort applies insertion sort to elements spaced by a gap and shrinks the gap; its running time depends on the chosen gap sequence.
short: Long-range swaps fix disorder early.
long: Long-range swaps fix disorder early. Shell's original halving sequence has O(n^2) worst case; other sequences give better proven bounds but no simple tight characterization for all practical choices.
proof: Each gapped pass is an insertion sort on n/g subsequences; combining pass bounds yields the sequence-dependent total.
consequence: Gap choice dominates performance, making Shell sort a favourite for empirical study.

title: Timsort Runs and Galloping
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Timsort detects naturally occurring ascending or descending runs, extends short runs by binary insertion sort and merges them with galloping.
short: It exploits order already present in real-world data.
long: It exploits order already present in real-world data. It is stable and uses O(n) auxiliary space in the worst case.
proof: Detected runs are merged with a balanced policy whose merge tree has depth O(log n); a single run needs only a linear scan.
consequence: Timsort is the default sort in Python and Java object arrays.

title: Timsort Worst-Case Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Timsort performs O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case and O(n) comparisons when the input already consists of one monotone run.
short: Adaptive merges never lose the logarithmic guarantee.
long: Adaptive merges never lose the logarithmic guarantee. Its run-stack invariants prevent badly balanced merges; galloping accelerates highly skewed merges.
proof: Maintaining run-length invariants bounds the merge tree depth by O(log n), and each level costs O(n).
consequence: The algorithm is both adaptive and worst-case optimal among comparison sorts.

title: Stability in Multi-Key Sorting
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Sorting by several keys can be done by stable sorting from the least significant key to the most significant, preserving earlier decisions.
short: Stable sorts compose into lexicographic order.
long: Stable sorts compose into lexicographic order. This is the radix principle applied to arbitrary key tuples, such as sorting cards by suit after sorting by rank.
proof: After the final stable pass by key 1, equal-key-1 items remain ordered by all earlier keys.
consequence: Stability is a practical requirement when records are sorted repeatedly on different fields.

title: Comparison Sort versus Counting Sort Regime
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Comparison sorting needs Omega(n log n) comparisons for arbitrary keys, while counting sort takes O(n+k) when keys lie in a range of size k.
short: Key structure, not comparison power, enables linear sorting.
long: Key structure, not comparison power, enables linear sorting. Counting sort trades generality for a range assumption and extra memory.
proof: The comparison bound applies only when the algorithm's decisions are comparisons; counting uses array indexing instead.
consequence: Choosing a sort requires understanding the key domain as well as the input size.

title: Sorting Network Comparator Model
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: A sorting network is a fixed sequence of compare-exchange operations whose behaviour does not depend on comparison outcomes.
short: The wiring is fixed in advance, ideal for hardware.
long: The wiring is fixed in advance, ideal for hardware. Depth is the number of sequential layers, and size is the total number of comparators.
proof: The zero-one principle says a network sorting all 0-1 inputs sorts arbitrary ordered inputs.
consequence: Sorting networks are used in hardware, GPUs and oblivious algorithms.

title: Bitonic Sort Network
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Bitonic sort builds and merges bitonic sequences in a network of depth O(log^2 n) and size O(n log^2 n).
short: Recursive bitonic merges give a regular parallel circuit.
long: Recursive bitonic merges give a regular parallel circuit. It requires n to be a power of two and performs the same comparisons regardless of input.
proof: A bitonic sequence of length n is merged with log n comparator stages, and log n merge levels are applied.
consequence: Its regularity makes it attractive on GPUs despite doing more work than optimal sorting networks.

title: Odd-Even Transposition Sort
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Odd-even transposition sort repeatedly compares and conditionally swaps adjacent pairs in alternating parity phases, sorting in n phases.
short: A simple linear-array sorting network.
long: A simple linear-array sorting network. Each phase is parallel across disjoint pairs, so it maps naturally to a processor array.
proof: After k phases, the k-th largest element has moved at least k positions toward its final end.
consequence: It is an easy-to-implement network for small parallel systems and for teaching sorting networks.

title: Sorting Network Depth Lower Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Any sorting network needs depth Omega(log n), and AKS networks achieve O(log n) depth with O(n log n) comparators.
short: Logarithmic depth is necessary and achievable, if not practical.
long: Logarithmic depth is necessary and achievable, if not practical. The AKS construction has enormous constants, so bitonic and merge-exchange networks win in practice.
proof: Each comparator layer at most doubles the number of distinct 0-1 outputs, so log n layers are needed to distinguish all n+1 threshold patterns.
consequence: It establishes the theoretical parallelism limit for comparison sorting.

title: Linear Search Lower Bound on Unsorted Data
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Finding whether a value occurs in an unsorted array of n items requires Theta(n) comparisons in the worst case.
short: Any unexamined element could be the target.
long: Any unexamined element could be the target. Sorted order or an index is necessary to beat linear search.
proof: After inspecting fewer than n elements, an adversary can place the target in an uninspected position.
consequence: This motivates hash tables and ordered indexes.

title: Binary Search on a Sorted Array
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Comparing the target with the middle element of a sorted array and discarding half the range finds it in O(log n) comparisons.
short: Halve the search interval at each step.
long: Halve the search interval at each step. It works on arrays, where midpoint access is O(1); on linked lists it is not efficient.
proof: The candidate interval size at most halves at each step, so at most ceil(log2(n+1)) comparisons are needed.
consequence: Binary search is the prototype for many monotonic search problems.

title: Binary Search Fails Without Sorted Order
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Applying binary search to the unsorted array [2, 9, 1, 4, 7] can discard the half containing the target and report a false miss.
short: Halving is valid only with a monotone predicate.
long: Halving is valid only with a monotone predicate. The algorithm implicitly uses the fact that all elements to the left of a larger midpoint are smaller.
proof: Searching for 1: midpoint 1 has value 9, so the left half is discarded even though it contains 1.
consequence: Always verify the monotonicity precondition before using binary search variants.

title: Interpolation Search Expected Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Interpolation search estimates the target position by value, giving O(log log n) expected comparisons for uniformly distributed sorted keys and O(n) worst case.
short: Use key values, not just positions, to guess the probe.
long: Use key values, not just positions, to guess the probe. It is advantageous for large, smoothly distributed numeric arrays.
proof: Linear interpolation lands within O(sqrt n) positions with constant probability, so expected remaining candidates shrink doubly exponentially.
consequence: It illustrates how distributional assumptions can improve over binary search.

title: Exponential Search for Unknown Bounds
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Doubling an index until it passes the target, then binary searching the last interval, takes O(log i) time where i is the target position.
short: Find the range first when the array bound is unknown.
long: Find the range first when the array bound is unknown. It is optimal for unbounded or infinite sorted arrays and for searching a sorted linked list with random access simulated.
proof: Doubling needs ceil(log2 i) probes, and binary search over the final interval of size at most i costs O(log i).
consequence: It underlies galloping in merge algorithms and search on unbounded streams.

title: Ternary Search on Unimodal Functions
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Evaluating a unimodal function at two interior points and discarding the side with the worse value locates the optimum in O(log(1/epsilon)) iterations for fixed precision.
short: Two probes per iteration shrink the containing interval.
long: Two probes per iteration shrink the containing interval. It requires strict unimodality; binary search on the derivative exploits the same idea.
proof: At least one of the outer thirds cannot contain the maximum, so the interval shrinks by a constant factor.
consequence: It is a standard one-dimensional optimisation technique.

title: Selection Problem and Order Statistics
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: The selection problem asks for the k-th smallest element, called the k-th order statistic, without necessarily sorting the whole array.
short: Finding one rank should be cheaper than full sorting.
long: Finding one rank should be cheaper than full sorting. The median corresponds to k = ceil(n/2); min and max are the extreme order statistics.
proof: Sorting produces all order statistics, so selection can be reduced to sorting but need not require it.
consequence: Selection algorithms achieve linear time where sorting needs n log n.

title: Quickselect Expected Linear Time
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Quickselect recurses only into the partition containing the desired rank, giving O(n) expected time and O(n^2) worst case.
short: Discard half the work by recursing on one side only.
long: Discard half the work by recursing on one side only. The expected recurrence is E[T(n)] <= E[T(n/2)] + O(n), whose solution is linear.
proof: A random pivot is equally likely to be any rank, making the expected subproblem size about n/2.
consequence: It is the fastest practical way to find a percentile in unsorted data.

title: Median-of-Medians Deterministic Selection
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Choosing a pivot as the median of groups of five and then the median of those medians yields worst-case O(n) selection.
short: A guaranteed good pivot gives a linear worst case.
long: A guaranteed good pivot gives a linear worst case. The constants are larger than quickselect's, so it is mainly of theoretical importance.
proof: The pivot exceeds at least 3 elements in half of the n/5 groups, so recursion is on at most 7n/10 elements; the recurrence solves to O(n).
consequence: It proves linear-time selection is possible without randomisation.

title: Order Statistic Tree for Rank Queries
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Augmenting a balanced tree with subtree sizes supports selecting the k-th smallest key and computing the rank of a key in O(log n) time.
short: Subtree counts turn paths into rank arithmetic.
long: Subtree counts turn paths into rank arithmetic. Updates must maintain the size field at each node along the modified path.
proof: At each node the left subtree size decides whether the k-th element lies left, at the node or right.
consequence: Order-statistic trees implement dynamic percentiles and rank aggregates.

title: k Smallest Elements with a Heap
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Inserting all n elements into a heap and extracting k minima takes O(n + k log n) time and O(n) space.
short: Build once, then pop exactly as many as needed.
long: Build once, then pop exactly as many as needed. Maintaining a max-heap of the k best seen instead uses O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
proof: Heapify is linear and each extraction costs the heap height.
consequence: The bounded-heap variant is the standard top-k streaming algorithm.

title: Top-k Heap versus Quickselect
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Quickselect finds k smallest in expected O(n) time, while a bounded heap takes O(n log k) but uses only O(k) space.
short: Speed versus streaming memory is the trade-off.
long: Speed versus streaming memory is the trade-off. A heap also works when k elements must be maintained under insertions.
proof: Quickselect partitions the whole array; a heap keeps only k candidates at any time.
consequence: Choose quickselect for offline arrays and bounded heaps for streams.

title: Boyer–Moore Majority Vote Algorithm
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: A single pass with a candidate and counter identifies the only possible element occurring more than n/2 times in O(n) time and O(1) space.
short: Paired cancellations leave the majority standing.
long: Paired cancellations leave the majority standing. A second pass is needed to confirm the candidate actually exceeds n/2 occurrences.
proof: Deleting pairs of distinct elements does not change a strict majority, so the final candidate is the only possible one.
consequence: It is the canonical constant-space streaming majority algorithm.

title: Tournament Method for Min and Max
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Finding both minimum and maximum by comparing pairs first takes at most 3n/2 - 2 comparisons instead of 2n - 2.
short: Compare in pairs, then scan winners and losers separately.
long: Compare in pairs, then scan winners and losers separately. The saving comes from extracting two comparisons' worth of information per pair.
proof: n/2 pair comparisons, then n/2-1 comparisons among winners and n/2-1 among losers.
consequence: It is the classic example of reducing constants by combining comparisons.

title: Staircase Search in a Sorted Matrix
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: In a matrix whose rows and columns are increasing, starting at the top-right corner and moving left or down finds a target in O(n+m) time.
short: Each step eliminates a whole row or column.
long: Each step eliminates a whole row or column. Binary searching each row would cost O(n log m), which can be worse.
proof: At position (i,j), moving down if the target is larger eliminates row i; moving left eliminates column j.
consequence: It demonstrates how two-dimensional monotonicity enables a linear traversal.

title: Binary Search on the Answer
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: When feasibility is monotone in a numeric parameter, binary search reduces optimisation to O(log R) feasibility tests over the answer range R.
short: Search the answer space, not the input array.
long: Search the answer space, not the input array. It requires a proof that if x is feasible then every smaller (or larger) x is feasible.
proof: Monotonicity means the predicate over the answer range is a step function with one boundary.
consequence: It solves problems such as minimal capacity, maximal minimum distance and integer square roots.

title: Searching a Sorted Array Lower Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Locating an arbitrary one of n sorted keys by comparisons requires Omega(log n) comparisons in the worst case.
short: Each comparison is binary, so n possibilities need log n bits.
long: Each comparison is binary, so n possibilities need log n bits. Binary search achieves the bound up to a constant.
proof: A comparison decision tree with n+1 possible outcomes has depth at least log2(n+1).
consequence: Binary search is asymptotically optimal in the comparison model.

title: k-Way Merge with a Binary Heap
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Merging k sorted lists with a min-heap of current heads takes O(n log k) time and O(k) extra space, where n is the total number of elements.
short: Keep only one candidate per list in the heap.
long: Keep only one candidate per list in the heap. Pairwise merging would take O(n log k) as well but with worse constants for uneven list sizes.
proof: Each of n outputs costs one extract-min and one insert, each O(log k).
consequence: k-way merging is the core of external merge sort and priority-queue-based schedulers.

title: Merging Two Sorted Arrays in Linear Time
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Two sorted arrays of total length n can be merged into one sorted array in O(n) time by advancing the smaller head.
short: A two-finger scan does the job.
long: A two-finger scan does the job. In-place variants without auxiliary storage are possible but more involved.
proof: At each step the smaller of the two heads is the next output element, so one pointer advances.
consequence: This linear merge is the workhorse of merge sort and union operations.

title: Adaptive Sorting and Inversion Distance
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Adaptive sorting algorithms run faster when the input is nearly sorted, with running time expressed in terms of a disorder measure such as the inversion count.
short: Presortedness is a resource that can be exploited.
long: Presortedness is a resource that can be exploited. Insertion sort needs O(n+I); more sophisticated adaptive mergesorts achieve O(n log(I/n+1)).
proof: Each inversion must be resolved by at least one comparison, and adaptive algorithms charge work to unresolved inversions.
consequence: Real-world data often has lots of existing order, making adaptive sorts attractive.

title: Entropy Form of the Sorting Lower Bound
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: The number of comparisons needed to sort n distinct items is at least log2(n!) = n log2 n - O(n), which equals the entropy of a uniform random permutation up to lower-order terms.
short: Sorting must identify one of n! equally likely permutations.
long: Sorting must identify one of n! equally likely permutations. With duplicates the lower bound drops to log2(n!/(n_1!...n_k!)).
proof: Stirling's approximation gives log2(n!) = n log2 n - n log2 e + O(log n).
consequence: Information theory and decision trees give the same optimality yardstick.

title: Tail Recursion in Quicksort
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Recursing on the smaller partition first and iterating on the larger one bounds quicksort's stack depth by O(log n) even in the worst case.
short: Keep the big subproblem on the stack frame you already have.
long: Keep the big subproblem on the stack frame you already have. The number of comparisons can still be Theta(n^2) without good pivots; only space is improved.
proof: Each recursive call at most halves the size of the remaining iterated problem, so depth is logarithmic.
consequence: It removes stack-overflow risk while preserving quicksort's speed.

title: Median-of-Three Pivot Heuristic
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Taking the median of three sampled elements as the pivot reduces the chance of a badly unbalanced partition compared with choosing one element.
short: A tiny sample makes extreme pivots less likely.
long: A tiny sample makes extreme pivots less likely. It still has Theta(n^2) worst case on adversarial input, so introsort adds a depth guard.
proof: The median of three is the middle-ranked element with higher probability than a single random element, improving expected split quality.
consequence: It is a standard low-cost heuristic in practical quicksort implementations.

title: Expected Versus Worst-Case Dictionary Search
subject: Sorting & Searching
statement: Hash tables give expected O(1) search under uniform hashing, while balanced trees give O(log n) worst case independent of the hash distribution.
short: Randomness buys speed but weakens the guarantee.
long: Randomness buys speed but weakens the guarantee. Universal hashing protects against adversarial keys but still yields only an expected bound.
proof: Chaining analysis uses uniformity of hash values; tree height bounds are deterministic.
consequence: Systems with latency guarantees often prefer trees or universal hashing with careful tail analysis.
