title: Breadth-First Search Explores by Distance
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Breadth-first search visits vertices in nondecreasing number of edges from the source, using a queue.
short: A FIFO queue processes the frontier one layer at a time.
long: A FIFO queue processes the frontier one layer at a time. Every vertex is enqueued once and every adjacency list is scanned once.
proof: The queue contains vertices at distance d followed by vertices at distance d+1, by induction on layers.
consequence: BFS yields shortest paths in unweighted graphs and the connected components of undirected graphs.

title: BFS Gives Unweighted Shortest Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In an unweighted graph, the parent pointers produced by BFS form shortest paths from the source to every reachable vertex.
short: First discovery is via a shortest route.
long: First discovery is via a shortest route. Edge weights can be handled by BFS only when all weights are equal or 0-1 BFS is used.
proof: If a shorter path existed, its penultimate vertex would be discovered in an earlier layer and would have enqueued v sooner.
consequence: BFS is the standard algorithm for hop-count distances and minimum-step puzzles.

title: DFS Discovery and Finish Times
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Depth-first search assigns discovery and finish times, and these intervals are either disjoint or nested.
short: DFS produces a nesting of recursive intervals.
long: DFS produces a nesting of recursive intervals. The parenthesis structure underlies topological sorting, SCC algorithms and bridge detection.
proof: A vertex is finished only after all descendants are finished, so intervals of descendant and non-descendant cannot partially overlap.
consequence: Finish-time order is a reusable primitive in many linear graph algorithms.

title: DFS Edge Classification in Directed Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: DFS classifies directed edges as tree, back, forward or cross according to the discovery and finish times of their endpoints.
short: Timestamps reveal cycles and ancestry.
long: Timestamps reveal cycles and ancestry. A directed graph is acyclic exactly when DFS finds no back edge.
proof: Edges to gray vertices are back edges, edges to descendants are forward edges, and edges to already finished non-descendants are cross edges.
consequence: The classification gives a linear cycle test and supports dependency analysis.

title: Topological Sort from DFS Finish Order
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting vertices by decreasing DFS finish time gives a topological order of a directed acyclic graph.
short: Finish later means depend on fewer predecessors.
long: Finish later means depend on fewer predecessors. Every edge u->v satisfies f(u) > f(v), so reversing finish time puts u before v.
proof: If u->v and u is discovered first, v finishes before u; if v is discovered first, the edge is a cross edge and v still finishes earlier.
consequence: It schedules tasks respecting precedence constraints in linear time.

title: Kahn's Algorithm for Topological Order
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly removing a vertex of in-degree zero and decreasing its neighbours' in-degrees yields a topological order, or detects a cycle.
short: Peel off vertices with no remaining prerequisites.
long: Peel off vertices with no remaining prerequisites. A queue or stack holds the current zero-in-degree set.
proof: A vertex can be output only after all predecessors are output, and in a DAG at least one zero-in-degree vertex exists at every step.
consequence: It is the standard implementation of dependency resolution and build ordering.

title: A Directed Graph Has a Topological Order iff It Is Acyclic
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A topological ordering exists for a directed graph if and only if the graph contains no directed cycle.
short: Cycles make precedence requirements impossible.
long: Cycles make precedence requirements impossible. A directed cycle requires each vertex on it to come before itself in any order.
proof: Necessity is immediate; sufficiency follows because a DAG always has a source, and induction removes it recursively.
consequence: Cycle detection and topological sorting are equivalent tasks.

title: Strongly Connected Components Partition a Digraph
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Strongly connected components are maximal vertex sets in which every vertex reaches every other, and they partition the vertices.
short: Mutual reachability is an equivalence relation.
long: Mutual reachability is an equivalence relation. Contracting components yields a directed acyclic graph, the condensation of the original graph.
proof: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of mutual reachability make it an equivalence relation whose classes partition V.
consequence: SCC decomposition simplifies analysis of reachability and cyclic dependencies.

title: Kosaraju's Two-Pass SCC Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Running DFS once on a digraph and then on its transpose in decreasing finish-time order identifies all strongly connected components in O(V+E) time.
short: Process the reversed graph in finish-time order.
long: Process the reversed graph in finish-time order. The first DFS on the transpose starting from the highest finish-time vertex isolates one source component of the condensation.
proof: Vertices of a component are discovered together in the second pass and no edge of the transpose leads outside before the component is complete.
consequence: It is a simple linear-time method for SCC decomposition.

title: Tarjan's Low-Link SCC Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A single DFS maintaining low-link values and a stack extracts each strongly connected component when its root is finished.
short: Back edges tell us when a DFS subtree closes into a component.
long: Back edges tell us when a DFS subtree closes into a component. low(v) is the smallest discovery time reachable from v via tree and at most one back edge.
proof: A component root has low-value equal to its own discovery time, so the stack segment above it forms exactly that component.
consequence: It computes SCCs in one pass without building the transpose.

title: Bridge Detection with Low Values
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In a DFS tree of an undirected graph, a tree edge (u,v) is a bridge exactly when low(v) > discovery(u).
short: No back edge from v's subtree reaches u or above.
long: No back edge from v's subtree reaches u or above. All non-tree edges in undirected DFS are back edges to an ancestor.
proof: If low(v) exceeds d(u), removing (u,v) separates v's subtree; otherwise a back edge provides an alternate route.
consequence: It finds vulnerable edges in networks in linear time.

title: Articulation Point Criterion
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In an undirected graph, a non-root DFS vertex u is an articulation point iff a child v satisfies low(v) >= discovery(u); the root is one iff it has more than one DFS child.
short: Cut vertices are detected by subtrees with no back route above them.
long: Cut vertices are detected by subtrees with no back route above them. The condition is evaluated during the same DFS that computes discovery and low values.
proof: If low(v) >= d(u), removing u disconnects v's subtree from the rest; the root separates each of its child subtrees.
consequence: It provides a linear-time test for network vulnerability.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm and Non-Negative Weights
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly settles the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance and relaxes its outgoing edges; it is correct when all edge weights are non-negative.
short: Greedy settlement is safe once no edge can reduce a settled distance.
long: Greedy settlement is safe once no edge can reduce a settled distance. With a Fibonacci heap the bound improves to O(E + V log V) amortised.
proof: If all weights are non-negative, any alternative path to the minimum tentative vertex via an unsettled vertex has length at least the current tentative distance.
consequence: It is the standard shortest-path method for road maps and network routing.

title: Dijkstra with a Binary Heap Complexity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Using a binary min-heap with decrease-key, Dijkstra runs in O((V+E) log V) time and O(V) extra space.
short: Each edge relaxation can cause a logarithmic heap update.
long: Each edge relaxation can cause a logarithmic heap update. With lazy duplicate insertions instead of decrease-key the bound becomes O(E log E), asymptotically comparable.
proof: There are at most E relaxations and V extract-mins, each costing O(log V).
consequence: This is the usual implementation choice for sparse graphs.

title: Dijkstra Fails on Negative Edges
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: With edges s->a of weight 1, s->b of weight 2 and b->a of weight -2, Dijkstra settles a at distance 1 and never corrects it to 0.
short: A settled vertex can later be reached more cheaply.
long: A settled vertex can later be reached more cheaply. Non-negativity is essential; Bellman-Ford handles negative edges but is slower.
proof: Dijkstra never reprocesses settled vertices, yet the path s-b-a has total weight 0 < 1.
consequence: Check edge signs before choosing a shortest-path algorithm.

title: Bellman-Ford and Negative Cycle Detection
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Relaxing all E edges V-1 times computes single-source shortest paths with negative edges, and one more pass detects a reachable negative cycle.
short: Repeated relaxation propagates improvements around cycles.
long: Repeated relaxation propagates improvements around cycles. If any distance still improves on the V-th pass, a negative cycle reachable from the source exists.
proof: A simple shortest path has at most V-1 edges, so after V-1 passes all distances are final unless a negative cycle permits endless improvement.
consequence: It is the method of choice when negative weights are possible and graphs are small or sparse.

title: Bellman-Ford Early Termination
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If a full relaxation pass makes no change, Bellman-Ford can stop before V-1 rounds.
short: No updates means the distances have converged.
long: No updates means the distances have converged. The best case is one pass plus a check, i.e. O(E), for favourable edge orderings.
proof: Once no edge can be relaxed, the distance labels satisfy the Bellman optimality conditions and are final.
consequence: Early exit makes Bellman-Ford competitive on many practical graphs.

title: SPFA Worst-Case Warning
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The short-path faster algorithm (SPFA), a queue-based Bellman-Ford variant, is often fast but has Theta(VE) worst-case running time.
short: Good average behaviour is not a worst-case guarantee.
long: Good average behaviour is not a worst-case guarantee. Specially constructed graphs force nearly every edge to be relaxed O(V) times.
proof: The queue-based ordering is still a form of repeated full relaxation, so the Bellman-Ford worst-case construction applies.
consequence: Use SPFA cautiously in latency-critical applications.

title: Floyd-Warshall All-Pairs Shortest Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths by allowing each vertex in turn as an intermediate point, taking O(V^3) time and O(V^2) space.
short: Intermediates are introduced one at a time.
long: Intermediates are introduced one at a time. It also detects negative cycles: a negative diagonal entry after the run signals one.
proof: After processing the first k vertices, d[i][j] is the shortest path whose internal vertices lie among those k; induction proves the update.
consequence: It is simple and fast enough for dense graphs of moderate size.

title: Floyd-Warshall In-Place Dynamic Program
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Floyd-Warshall recurrence needs only a single distance matrix because iteration k never changes entries already used for earlier intermediates.
short: The k-th row and column are reused during step k without a second matrix.
long: The k-th row and column are reused during step k without a second matrix. Predecessor matrices can be maintained alongside distances to reconstruct paths.
proof: Since intermediate k is new, the shortest path using it decomposes into two paths with smaller intermediates already finalised.
consequence: The algorithm's memory footprint is just quadratic in the number of vertices.

title: Johnson's Algorithm for Sparse Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Johnson reweights edges using potentials from one Bellman-Ford run, then runs Dijkstra from every vertex, taking O(VE + V^2 log V) time.
short: Make weights non-negative once, then reuse fast Dijkstra.
long: Make weights non-negative once, then reuse fast Dijkstra. The potential h(v)=dist(s,v) yields non-negative reduced weights w'(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(u)-h(v) when no negative cycle exists.
proof: The triangle inequality gives w'(u,v) >= 0, and reduced path costs differ from original ones only by endpoint potentials, preserving shortest paths.
consequence: It is asymptotically better than Floyd-Warshall on sparse graphs with possibly negative edges.

title: Shortest Paths in a DAG
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Relaxing edges in topological order computes single-source shortest paths in a directed acyclic graph in O(V+E) time, even with negative edge weights.
short: Topological order already respects every dependency.
long: Topological order already respects every dependency. Longest paths and critical-path analysis use the same recurrence with maximisation.
proof: When an edge u->v is relaxed, all paths into u have already been processed, so dist[u] is final.
consequence: DAGs admit faster and more general shortest-path algorithms than general graphs.

title: A* Optimality with Admissible Heuristics
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A* search returns an optimal path when the heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost.
short: Optimistic estimates cannot hide a better route.
long: Optimistic estimates cannot hide a better route. Runtime depends strongly on heuristic quality; with h = 0, A* degenerates to Dijkstra.
proof: Before expanding a node with optimal cost C, some node on an optimal path with estimate at most C would have smaller f-value, so A* expands it first.
consequence: Admissible heuristics such as Manhattan distance make grid pathfinding fast and correct.

title: A* Consistency Avoids Reopening
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If an A* heuristic satisfies h(u) <= c(u,v) + h(v) for every edge, the first time a node is expanded is optimal and no reopening is needed.
short: Consistency makes f-values monotone along paths.
long: Consistency makes f-values monotone along paths. Consistency implies admissibility but not conversely.
proof: Along any path, f-values are nondecreasing, so a node cannot later be reached with a smaller f-value.
consequence: Consistent heuristics simplify implementations and bound the number of expansions.

title: Bidirectional Search Reduces Frontier Size
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Searching simultaneously from the source and target can reduce explored nodes from O(b^d) to about O(b^{d/2}) when both directions are available.
short: Two shallower searches meet in the middle.
long: Two shallower searches meet in the middle. It requires reversible edges or symmetric state transitions and a reliable meeting test.
proof: Each side explores to depth d/2, so the number of generated states is roughly twice b^{d/2}.
consequence: It is used in route planning and puzzle solving to accelerate breadth-first searches.

title: BFS on Implicit State Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: BFS works when vertices are states generated on the fly rather than stored explicitly, provided neighbours can be enumerated and duplicates detected.
short: Build the graph as you explore it.
long: Build the graph as you explore it. A visited set keyed by canonical state prevents revisits in graphs with converging transitions.
proof: The queue discipline depends only on neighbour generation, not on an explicit adjacency matrix.
consequence: This is the standard model for solving puzzles, protocol reachability and game states.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Cut Property
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For any cut, a minimum-weight edge crossing it belongs to every minimum spanning tree if its weight is strictly smaller than all other crossing edges.
short: The cheapest bridge across a divide is safe to include.
long: The cheapest bridge across a divide is safe to include. Ties can make some but not all minimum crossing edges part of an MST.
proof: If an MST omits e, adding e creates a cycle crossing the cut; removing a heavier crossing edge yields a lighter tree.
consequence: The cut property justifies Kruskal's and Prim's greedy choices.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Cycle Property
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The heaviest edge on any cycle cannot belong to a minimum spanning tree if its weight is strictly larger than every other edge on that cycle.
short: An over-heavy cycle edge is never needed.
long: An over-heavy cycle edge is never needed. With equal weights the statement requires the unique-heaviest condition.
proof: If an MST contained e, removing e splits the tree; some other cycle edge reconnects the parts with smaller weight.
consequence: The cycle property justifies reverse-delete algorithms.

title: Kruskal's Algorithm with Union-Find
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting edges by weight and adding each edge that connects different components builds a minimum spanning tree in O(E log E) time.
short: Greedily add the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle.
long: Greedily add the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. Union-find tests component membership; ties in weight are handled arbitrarily.
proof: When an edge is added it is the cheapest crossing the cut between its component and the rest, so the cut property applies.
consequence: Kruskal is simple and efficient for sparse graphs.

title: Prim's Algorithm with a Priority Queue
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Growing a single tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to an outside vertex yields an MST in O(E log V) with a binary heap.
short: Expand the frontier one vertex at a time.
long: Expand the frontier one vertex at a time. With a Fibonacci heap the amortised bound is O(E + V log V).
proof: The chosen edge is cheapest across the cut separating the current tree from unvisited vertices, so the cut property applies.
consequence: Prim is efficient on dense graphs and natural when starting from a given vertex.

title: Prim with Fibonacci Heap Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Using a Fibonacci heap, Prim's algorithm runs in O(E + V log V) amortised time.
short: Cheap decrease-key operations accelerate dense MST construction.
long: Cheap decrease-key operations accelerate dense MST construction. Each edge triggers at most one decrease-key, which is O(1) amortised in a Fibonacci heap.
proof: There are O(E) heap updates and O(V) extract-mins costing O(log V) amortised.
consequence: This matches the best known bounds for dense-graph MST.

title: Boruvka's Parallel MST Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Boruvka repeatedly adds the cheapest outgoing edge of every component, reducing the number of components by at least half in each phase.
short: Every component simultaneously picks its cheapest exit.
long: Every component simultaneously picks its cheapest exit. The phase structure makes it attractive in parallel and distributed settings.
proof: At least half of the components merge in each round because each chosen edge merges two components.
consequence: It is one of the oldest MST algorithms and still used in parallel implementations.

title: Reverse-Delete MST Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting edges from most to least expensive and deleting an edge whenever the graph stays connected leaves a minimum spanning tree.
short: Discard the most expensive edge that is not essential.
long: Discard the most expensive edge that is not essential. A straightforward connectivity test per edge makes it slower than Kruskal or Prim.
proof: A deleted edge is the heaviest on some cycle, so it cannot be in an MST by the cycle property.
consequence: It is a clean illustration of the duality between cut and cycle properties.

title: Distinct Edge Weights Imply Unique MST
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If all edge weights in a connected graph are distinct, the minimum spanning tree is unique.
short: No tie means every greedy choice is forced.
long: No tie means every greedy choice is forced. With equal weights multiple MSTs can coexist, but Kruskal still produces one valid MST.
proof: If two MSTs differed, take the lightest edge where they differ; the cut property forces it into both, a contradiction.
consequence: Uniqueness simplifies sensitivity analysis and algorithm correctness arguments.

title: Every MST Is a Minimum Bottleneck Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every minimum spanning tree is also a minimum bottleneck spanning tree, minimising the largest edge weight, though the converse need not hold.
short: Minimising total weight also minimises the worst edge.
long: Minimising total weight also minimises the worst edge. A bottleneck-optimal tree can still have larger total weight than an MST.
proof: If a tree had a smaller maximum edge, the MST edge introducing that bottleneck would violate the cut property.
consequence: MST algorithms can be reused for bottleneck connectivity problems.

title: MST Algorithm Choice by Graph Density
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Kruskal is O(E log E) and often best for sparse graphs, while Prim with a simple array is O(V^2) and better for dense graphs.
short: Edge sorting versus vertex scanning.
long: Edge sorting versus vertex scanning. Fibonacci-heap Prim improves dense cases to O(E + V log V).
proof: Kruskal's cost is dominated by sorting E edges; array-based Prim scans all V vertices for each of V additions.
consequence: Graph representation and density determine the best MST implementation.

title: MST Is Not a Shortest-Path Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An MST rooted at s need not give shortest paths from s; with edges s-a of weight 1, a-b of weight 1 and s-b of weight 1.5, the MST uses s-a and a-b, so its path to b costs 2 while the shortest path costs 1.5.
short: Minimising total tree weight is a different objective.
long: Minimising total tree weight is a different objective. Conversely, a shortest-path tree need not be a minimum spanning tree.
proof: MST minimises sum of edges; shortest-path tree minimises root distances, and no inclusion relation holds in general.
consequence: Use Dijkstra for distances and MST algorithms for network-wide cost minimisation.

title: Odd Cycles Characterise Bipartite Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
short: Two-colouring fails exactly when an odd cycle forces a conflict.
long: Two-colouring fails exactly when an odd cycle forces a conflict. BFS or DFS colouring detects such a conflict in O(V+E) time.
proof: Colouring by parity of distance from a source is consistent unless an edge joins same-parity vertices, which creates an odd cycle.
consequence: Bipartiteness tests are linear and underpin bipartite matching applications.

title: Bipartite Matching Problem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A matching in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared endpoints; maximum matching maximises their number.
short: Pair up left and right vertices without conflicts.
long: Pair up left and right vertices without conflicts. It models assignment of jobs to workers, students to projects and many other pairing tasks.
proof: The degree constraint encodes that each vertex can be used at most once.
consequence: It is one of the most tractable and widely used combinatorial optimisation problems.

title: Augmenting Paths for Bipartite Matching
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly finding an augmenting path—an unmatched-starting, unmatched-ending alternating path—increases matching size by one until none exists.
short: Flip a path to add one more pair.
long: Flip a path to add one more pair. A BFS-based search for augmenting paths gives the O(VE) Hopcroft–Karp predecessor algorithm.
proof: Berge's lemma says a matching is maximum iff it admits no augmenting path.
consequence: It provides a simple polynomial algorithm for bipartite matching.

title: Hopcroft–Karp Complexity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Hopcroft–Karp finds a maximum bipartite matching in O(E sqrt(V)) time by finding maximal sets of shortest augmenting paths in each phase.
short: Batch augmentations shorten the number of phases.
long: Batch augmentations shorten the number of phases. Each phase uses DFS layered searches and augments along many vertex-disjoint paths at once.
proof: After sqrt(V) phases, augmenting path lengths have grown enough that at most sqrt(V) further phases remain, with O(E) work each.
consequence: It is the standard efficient algorithm for large bipartite matchings.

title: König's Matching–Vertex Cover Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover.
short: Bipartite duality makes two different problems equal.
long: Bipartite duality makes two different problems equal. This equality fails in general graphs, where vertex cover is NP-hard.
proof: Given a maximum matching, the set of vertices reachable by alternating paths from unmatched left vertices yields a vertex cover of the same size.
consequence: It gives a polynomial algorithm for minimum vertex cover in bipartite graphs and implies integrality of the LP relaxation.

title: Hungarian Algorithm for Assignment
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Hungarian algorithm solves the n by n minimum-cost perfect assignment problem in O(n^3) time using primal-dual label updates.
short: Dual potentials guide augmentations to an optimal assignment.
long: Dual potentials guide augmentations to an optimal assignment. It is equivalent to shortest augmenting paths in a bipartite matching with reduced costs.
proof: Maintaining feasible dual labels and complementary slackness for the current matching yields optimality when all vertices are matched.
consequence: It underlies optimal assignment in operations research and tracking systems.

title: Gale–Shapley Stable Marriage
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Deferred acceptance produces a stable matching in O(n^2) time, with all proposers receiving their best stable partners.
short: Proposals plus rejections converge to a stable pairing.
long: Proposals plus rejections converge to a stable pairing. The version where men propose is men-optimal and women-pessimal among stable matchings.
proof: Rejections only move down preference lists, and termination with no unmatched proposer and no blocking pair follows.
consequence: It is used in school choice, medical residency matching and stable roommate variants.

title: Greedy Fails for General Graph Matching
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Choosing the shortest or heaviest edge greedily can yield a non-maximum matching in a general graph.
short: Local pairing decisions can block better global pairings.
long: Local pairing decisions can block better global pairings. In a path of four vertices with centre edge heavy, taking the centre prevents matching both ends.
proof: On vertices a-b-c-d with edges ab, bc, cd, choosing bc leaves only one more edge possible, total 1; choosing ab and cd gives 2.
consequence: General maximum matching requires augmenting-path algorithms such as Edmonds' blossom algorithm.

title: Flow Networks and s-t Cuts
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A flow network is a directed graph with capacities, and an s-t cut partitions vertices with s on one side and t on the other; the cut capacity is the sum of outgoing edge capacities.
short: Cuts are bottlenecks separating source from sink.
long: Cuts are bottlenecks separating source from sink. A feasible flow satisfies capacity constraints and conservation at all vertices except s and t.
proof: Every s-t path crosses every cut, so cut capacity bounds the total achievable flow.
consequence: Flows and cuts are dual objects underlying network optimisation.

title: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In any flow network, the value of a maximum flow equals the capacity of a minimum s-t cut.
short: The best flow is exactly limited by the tightest bottleneck.
long: The best flow is exactly limited by the tightest bottleneck. The residual graph at maximum flow identifies the minimum cut as vertices reachable from s.
proof: Flow across any cut equals flow value, giving weak duality; at maximum flow no augmenting path remains, so reachable set forms a cut whose capacity equals the flow.
consequence: It justifies flow-based algorithms and gives constructive minimum cuts.

title: Ford–Fulkerson Method and Integrality
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly augmenting along residual paths terminates with a maximum flow for integer capacities, using at most O(E |f*|) augmentations.
short: Integral capacities keep every augmentation progress.
long: Integral capacities keep every augmentation progress. With irrational capacities the method need not terminate or converge to the maximum.
proof: Each augmentation increases flow value by at least one unit when capacities are integers, and the value is bounded by the minimum cut.
consequence: Integrality explains why matching and flow yield integer solutions in combinatorial problems.

title: Edmonds–Karp Polynomial Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Choosing shortest augmenting paths by BFS in Ford–Fulkerson gives O(VE^2) time.
short: Shortest paths limit how often an edge can become critical.
long: Shortest paths limit how often an edge can become critical. It was the first strongly polynomial max-flow algorithm.
proof: The distance from s to any vertex in the residual graph never decreases, and a given edge can be saturated at most O(V) times, giving O(VE) augmentations of cost O(E).
consequence: It guarantees polynomial time independent of capacity magnitudes.

title: Dinic's Blocking Flow Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Dinic builds level graphs and pushes blocking flows, running in O(V^2 E) in general and O(E sqrt(E)) on unit networks.
short: Layered networks make augmentations efficient.
long: Layered networks make augmentations efficient. Current-arc pointers avoid rescanning saturated edges within a phase.
proof: Each phase increases the level of the bottleneck structure, giving at most V phases, and a blocking flow is found in O(VE) via DFS with current arcs.
consequence: It is fast in practice and the basis of many modern max-flow implementations.

title: Push-Relabel Maximum Flow
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Push-relabel avoids augmenting paths by maintaining a preflow and local height labels, with a FIFO implementation taking O(V^3) time.
short: Push excess locally and relabel stuck vertices.
long: Push excess locally and relabel stuck vertices. The highest-label variant and gap heuristics make it very fast in practice.
proof: Relabels and pushes are bounded by potential arguments over heights and excesses, giving a cubic bound for the FIFO variant.
consequence: It is a leading practical approach for large max-flow instances.

title: Bipartite Matching as a Flow Problem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Directing source-to-left and right-to-sink edges with unit capacities reduces bipartite matching to maximum flow.
short: Flow integrality automatically gives integral matchings.
long: Flow integrality automatically gives integral matchings. A unit-capacity network can be solved by Dinic in O(E sqrt(V)).
proof: Integral unit flows select a set of left-right edges with no repeated endpoint, exactly a matching.
consequence: Flow algorithms provide a general route to matching and its weighted variants.

title: Menger's Theorem and Disjoint Paths
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths between two vertices equals the minimum number of vertices separating them.
short: Connectivity equals the size of the smallest cut.
long: Connectivity equals the size of the smallest cut. The edge version states equality between edge-disjoint paths and edge cuts; both follow from max-flow min-cut with node splitting.
proof: Model vertex capacities by splitting vertices, apply max-flow min-cut and map integral flows to disjoint paths.
consequence: It links graph connectivity to flow and underpins network reliability analysis.

title: Node Splitting for Vertex Capacities
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Replacing each vertex v by v_in -> v_out with capacity c_v converts vertex-capacitated cuts into ordinary edge cuts.
short: Vertex limits become edge limits.
long: Vertex limits become edge limits. Incoming edges enter v_in and outgoing edges leave v_out; source and sink get infinite capacity.
proof: Any finite cut must cut a split edge to disconnect that vertex, paying exactly its vertex capacity.
consequence: It reduces minimum vertex cut and disjoint-path problems to standard max flow.

title: Gomory–Hu Cut Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An undirected graph has a weighted tree on its vertices such that the minimum cut between any pair equals the minimum edge weight on their tree path.
short: All pairwise min cuts fit in one tree.
long: All pairwise min cuts fit in one tree. It can be built with n-1 max-flow computations.
proof: Recursively find a minimum s-t cut, contract sides into tree nodes and recurse within each side.
consequence: It compactly represents global connectivity information.

title: Greedy Graph Coloring Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Ordering vertices arbitrarily and assigning the smallest available colour uses at most Delta+1 colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: At most Delta neighbours forbid colours at each step.
long: At most Delta neighbours forbid colours at each step. Better orderings can use fewer colours, but finding the chromatic number is NP-hard.
proof: When colouring a vertex, at most Delta colours are used by already coloured neighbours.
consequence: It is a simple constructive upper bound used in register allocation heuristics.

title: Brooks' Theorem on Chromatic Number
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A connected graph with maximum degree Delta >= 3 has chromatic number at most Delta, unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle.
short: The naive Delta+1 bound is almost always improvable.
long: The naive Delta+1 bound is almost always improvable. The exceptional graphs indeed require Delta+1 colours.
proof: A careful greedy ordering after removing a suitable pair of non-adjacent neighbours avoids the forbidden colour at each step.
consequence: It sharpens the basic greedy bound and classifies the extremal cases.

title: Vizing's Edge Colouring Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The edges of any simple graph can be coloured with either Delta or Delta+1 colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: Edge colouring has only two possible answers.
long: Edge colouring has only two possible answers. Deciding which case holds is NP-hard in general, but bipartite graphs always need only Delta colours.
proof: Vizing's alternating-path argument extends a partial colouring one edge at a time.
consequence: It is a sharp structural result with applications to scheduling and matchings.

title: Eulerian Circuit Degree Characterization
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit iff every vertex has even degree, and an Eulerian trail iff exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree.
short: You can close a tour exactly when degrees are even.
long: You can close a tour exactly when degrees are even. Each visit to a vertex consumes one entering and one leaving edge.
proof: Necessity follows from pairing arrivals and departures; sufficiency follows by Hierholzer's splicing of cycles.
consequence: It solves route-inspection and snowplough problems.

title: Hierholzer's Euler Tour Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Following unused edges until returning to the start and splicing detoured cycles produces an Eulerian tour in O(E) time.
short: Splice closed walks into a growing circuit.
long: Splice closed walks into a growing circuit. A stack of vertices with backtracking yields the tour in reverse order.
proof: Every edge is used exactly once, and splicing a closed walk at a repeated vertex preserves the Eulerian property.
consequence: It is the standard linear-time construction for Euler tours.

title: Hamiltonian Cycle Is NP-Complete
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Deciding whether an undirected graph has a Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete.
short: Finding a tour through every vertex is computationally hard.
long: Finding a tour through every vertex is computationally hard. The related travelling salesman decision problem is NP-complete as well.
proof: Membership in NP is verified by a certificate cycle; reductions from SAT or 3-SAT establish hardness.
consequence: Exact exponential algorithms and approximation heuristics are used instead.

title: Held–Karp TSP Dynamic Programming
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Subset DP computes exact shortest Hamiltonian tours in O(2^n n^2) time and O(2^n n) space.
short: Remember the best path for each visited subset and endpoint.
long: Remember the best path for each visited subset and endpoint. It is exponential but vastly better than enumerating n! permutations.
proof: dp[S][v] is the shortest path visiting exactly S and ending at v; extending by one unvisited vertex gives the recurrence.
consequence: It is the standard exact method for TSP instances with up to a few dozen cities.

title: MST Doubling Gives a 2-Approximation for TSP
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For metric TSP, doubling an MST and shortcutting repeated vertices gives a tour of at most twice the optimum.
short: A spanning tree skeleton can be walked around cheaply.
long: A spanning tree skeleton can be walked around cheaply. The triangle inequality is needed for shortcutting not to increase cost.
proof: The doubled tree has cost 2 w(MST) <= 2 OPT, and metric shortcuts only reduce the length.
consequence: It is a simple, practical approximation guarantee for metric instances.

title: Christofides 3/2-Approximation
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For metric TSP, adding a minimum perfect matching on odd-degree vertices of an MST yields a tour within 3/2 of optimal.
short: Fix the parity defects of the tree with a cheap matching.
long: Fix the parity defects of the tree with a cheap matching. It improves the classic 2-approximation and was the best general guarantee for decades.
proof: The matching costs at most OPT/2 by the cut and matching structure of an optimal tour, and the resulting Eulerian multigraph is shortcutted.
consequence: It is a landmark result in approximation algorithms.

title: Maximal Matching 2-Approximates Vertex Cover
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Taking both endpoints of every edge in a maximal matching gives a vertex cover of size at most twice the minimum.
short: A maximal matching certifies a near-optimal cover.
long: A maximal matching certifies a near-optimal cover. The approximation ratio is tight for this simple algorithm.
proof: Every edge of a minimum cover must touch one matched edge, so OPT is at least the matching size, while the cover has twice that size.
consequence: Vertex cover is approximable even though it is NP-hard.

title: Clique and Independent Set Complementarity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A set is a clique in G exactly when it is an independent set in the complement of G.
short: Cliques and independent sets are the same problem in complementary graphs.
long: Cliques and independent sets are the same problem in complementary graphs. Both problems are NP-complete, and both are hard to approximate within n^{1-epsilon}.
proof: Adjacency is inverted in the complement, so pairwise adjacency becomes pairwise non-adjacency.
consequence: Reductions between the two problems are immediate.

title: Graph Isomorphism Complexity Status
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Graph isomorphism is in NP but is not known to be in P or NP-complete; Babai gave a quasipolynomial-time algorithm.
short: Its complexity sits in a rare unresolved middle ground.
long: Its complexity sits in a rare unresolved middle ground. Practical tools use refinement and backtracking, such as the Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy.
proof: A permutation mapping is an easily verified certificate, and Babai's group-theoretic algorithm runs in exp((log n)^{O(1)}) time.
consequence: It is a central open problem with implications for symmetry detection and chemistry.

title: Bitset Transitive Closure
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Representing reachability rows as bit vectors computes the transitive closure in O(n^3 / w) machine operations for word size w.
short: Warshall's update becomes a bitwise OR.
long: Warshall's update becomes a bitwise OR. The space is O(n^2 / w) words, and it is fast for moderate n on 64-bit machines.
proof: Row update R[i] |= R[k] whenever R[i][k] is set operates on w bits at once.
consequence: Bitset acceleration makes dense reachability queries practical.

title: Repeated Squaring for Reachability
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Boolean adjacency matrix raised to the n-th power under Boolean matrix multiplication gives the transitive closure.
short: Matrix powers count walk lengths.
long: Matrix powers count walk lengths. Repeated squaring needs O(log n) Boolean matrix products, each reducible to fast matrix multiplication.
proof: An entry of A^k is 1 exactly when a walk of length k exists, and any reachable pair has a walk of length at most n-1.
consequence: It links reachability to the theory of fast matrix multiplication.

title: Planar Graph Edge Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A simple planar graph with n >= 3 vertices has at most 3n - 6 edges, and at most 2n - 4 if it is bipartite.
short: Euler's formula limits how dense a planar graph can be.
long: Euler's formula limits how dense a planar graph can be. Consequently planar graphs are sparse and admit efficient algorithms.
proof: Euler's formula n - m + f = 2 and the fact that each face has at least 3 (or 4) sides give the inequality.
consequence: Planarity implies linear space and often linear-time algorithms.

title: Linear-Time Planarity Testing
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Hopcroft–Tarjan algorithm tests planarity and produces an embedding in O(V) time.
short: Depth-first search structure characterises embeddability.
long: Depth-first search structure characterises embeddability. It relies on partitioning DFS edges into interlacement classes to check whether conflicts can be resolved.
proof: The algorithm constructs an embedding incrementally and proves that any failure implies non-planarity by Kuratowski's theorem.
consequence: Planarity can be recognised as cheaply as reading the graph.

title: Five Colour Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every planar graph can be coloured with at most five colours.
short: Euler's formula guarantees a low-degree vertex for induction.
long: Euler's formula guarantees a low-degree vertex for induction. The four-colour theorem strengthens this to four but has a much harder proof.
proof: A planar graph has a vertex of degree at most 5; removing it, colouring recursively and using Kempe chains handles the degree-5 case.
consequence: It gives an elementary colouring guarantee for maps and planar networks.

title: Bipartite Edge Colouring Needs Delta Colours
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every bipartite graph has an edge colouring with exactly Delta colours, where Delta is the maximum degree.
short: Bipartite structure eliminates Vizing's extra colour.
long: Bipartite structure eliminates Vizing's extra colour. Such a colouring can be found in polynomial time by repeated matching on a regularised graph.
proof: Embed the bipartite graph in a Delta-regular bipartite multigraph, decompose into Delta perfect matchings by Hall's theorem and restrict.
consequence: It yields optimal timetabling for bipartite conflict structures.

title: Minimum Cut for Image Segmentation
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Binary image segmentation can be formulated as an s-t minimum cut where unary terms attach pixels to labels and pairwise terms penalise label disagreements.
short: Graph cuts optimise a common vision energy.
long: Graph cuts optimise a common vision energy. Submodular pairwise terms make the energy exactly minimisable by max flow.
proof: The cut capacity equals the sum of unary and pairwise costs under the standard construction, so a minimum cut minimises the energy.
consequence: Max-flow algorithms are core tools in computer vision.
wiki: Graph cuts in computer vision and artificial intelligence

title: Offline Dynamic Connectivity over Time
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For a known sequence of edge insertions and deletions, a segment tree over time intervals with rollback union-find answers connectivity queries in O(E log T alpha(V)).
short: Assign each edge to time segments and process recursively.
long: Assign each edge to time segments and process recursively. Rollback union-find restores state when backtracking, avoiding persistent copies.
proof: Each edge appears in O(log T) segment-tree nodes; at a leaf all active edges have been unioned exactly once.
consequence: It solves dynamic connectivity efficiently when the whole update sequence is known in advance.

title: Big-O Upper Bound Definition
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are constants c > 0 and n0 such that 0 <= f(n) <= c g(n) for all n >= n0.
short: Eventually f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g.
long: Eventually f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g. Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound and is the standard language for worst-case running times.
proof: Given witnesses c and n0, the inequality holds for every larger n by definition.
consequence: It suppresses machine constants and low-order terms so algorithms can be compared structurally.

title: Big-Omega and Big-Theta Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = Omega(g(n)) means g(n) = O(f(n)), and f(n) = Theta(g(n)) means both f = O(g) and f = Omega(g).
short: Theta pins the growth rate from both sides.
long: Theta pins the growth rate from both sides. Saying an algorithm is Theta(n log n) is stronger than saying it is O(n^2).
proof: Combining the two sets of witnesses c1 and c2 gives the two-sided inequality for large n.
consequence: Theta notation expresses tight bounds such as the exact order of merge sort.

title: Little-o and Strict Asymptotic Dominance
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n)/g(n) tends to zero, so g grows strictly faster than f.
short: The ratio vanishes rather than staying bounded.
long: The ratio vanishes rather than staying bounded. For example log n = o(n^epsilon) for every epsilon > 0.
proof: The limit definition is equivalent to f(n) <= epsilon g(n) eventually for every epsilon > 0.
consequence: It distinguishes tight Theta bounds from strictly weaker upper bounds.

title: Worst, Average and Amortised Costs
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Worst-case cost maximises over inputs, average-case cost averages over an input distribution, and amortised cost averages over a sequence of operations.
short: Three different ways to summarise a running time.
long: Three different ways to summarise a running time. An O(1) amortised bound can hide an O(n) single operation; an average-case bound depends on a distributional assumption.
proof: The three quantities are defined by different aggregations of the same per-operation or per-input cost.
consequence: Stating which notion is meant prevents misinterpretation of algorithmic guarantees.

title: Unit-Cost RAM Model
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The RAM model assumes a sequential machine in which each arithmetic, comparison and memory access takes one time unit.
short: Count operations, not machine cycles.
long: Count operations, not machine cycles. It ignores caches, pipelining and word-size overflow, making analysis tractable.
proof: The model is a definition: each primitive instruction is charged unit cost.
consequence: Most textbook O-notation bounds are stated in this model.

title: Word RAM and Transdichotomous Model
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The word RAM allows constant-time operations on w-bit words with w at least log n, so an entire input index fits in one word.
short: Words scale with problem size.
long: Words scale with problem size. It enables bit-parallel tricks and integer sorting bounds unavailable in the comparison model.
proof: Setting word size proportional to log n lets the machine address any input location and pack log n bits.
consequence: It is the standard theoretical model for integer algorithms and succinct data structures.

title: Bit Complexity versus Arithmetic Complexity
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Treating arithmetic as unit-cost can hide the bit operations needed for large numbers; multiplying two n-bit integers costs O(n^2) naively.
short: Big integers make constant-time arithmetic inaccurate.
long: Big integers make constant-time arithmetic inaccurate. Fast multiplication algorithms reduce this, but the distinction remains important in cryptography and exact computation.
proof: Schoolbook multiplication forms n^2 partial products of single bits.
consequence: Bit complexity is the right model when operands grow with the input size.

title: Aggregate Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The aggregate method bounds the total cost of m operations directly and divides by m to obtain the amortised cost per operation.
short: Prove a total bound, then average.
long: Prove a total bound, then average. It works best when operations are similar, as with dynamic-array resizing.
proof: If the total cost of any m operations is O(mg(n)), the average cost is O(g(n)).
consequence: It is the simplest of the three standard amortised-analysis methods.

title: Accounting Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The accounting method charges each operation a fixed fee, storing surplus credit on objects to pay for later expensive operations.
short: Overcharge cheap operations to fund rare costly ones.
long: Overcharge cheap operations to fund rare costly ones. The credit invariant must hold after every operation.
proof: If total charged fees are an upper bound on total actual cost and credit never goes negative, the amortised bound follows.
consequence: It gives an intuitive proof of amortised O(1) for push and pop with multipop.

title: Potential Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The potential method defines a nonnegative function Phi on states and charges operation i the actual cost plus Phi(state_i) - Phi(state_{i-1}).
short: Stored potential pays for future work.
long: Stored potential pays for future work. Because the potential telescopes, the total amortised cost exceeds the total actual cost by at most the initial potential.
proof: Summing the charges gives sum c_i + Phi_m - Phi_0, which is at least sum c_i when Phi_0 = 0 and Phi_m >= 0.
consequence: Potentials handle complex structures such as splay trees and Fibonacci heaps.

title: Multipop Stack Amortised Bound
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A stack supporting push, pop and multipop(k) in which multipop removes up to k elements has O(1) amortised cost per operation when the potential is the stack size.
short: A multipop pays for itself by releasing stored potential.
long: A multipop pays for itself by releasing stored potential. A multipop can cost O(n) in one step but decreases the potential by the same amount.
proof: Amortised cost of multipop is k + (-k) = O(1), while push costs 1 + 1 and pop costs 1 - 1.
consequence: It is the canonical first example of the potential method.

title: Substitution Method for Recurrences
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The substitution method guesses a bound on T(n) and verifies it by induction, possibly subtracting a lower-order term to make the induction go through.
short: Guess, then prove by induction.
long: Guess, then prove by induction. Changing variables can handle recurrences with floors and ceilings.
proof: Assume the bound for smaller arguments, substitute into the recurrence and confirm it for n.
consequence: It proves bounds for recurrences not covered by standard templates.

title: Recursion Tree Method
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Drawing a recursion tree and summing work level by level converts divide-and-conquer recurrences into geometric or arithmetic sums.
short: Add up the cost at each depth.
long: Add up the cost at each depth. It gives intuition even when a formal induction is still needed to confirm the bound.
proof: Each node's cost is the nonrecursive work for its subproblem; summing over all nodes at a level and over levels yields T(n).
consequence: It explains why the shape of f(n) determines the asymptotic solution.

title: Work Accumulation Across Recursive Levels
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), the total cost is governed by whether f decreases, stays level with, or grows relative to n^{log_b a} across levels.
short: Leaf count versus per-level cost decides the winner.
long: Leaf count versus per-level cost decides the winner. This is the mechanism behind the three common cases of divide-and-conquer recurrences.
proof: At level i there are a^i subproblems of size n/b^i, so per-level work is a^i f(n/b^i) and the sequence is compared with a geometric progression.
consequence: It builds intuition for recurrence-solving theorems without memorising their statements.

title: Akra–Bazzi General Recurrence Method
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For T(n) = sum_i a_i T(b_i n) + g(n) with a_i > 0 and 0 < b_i < 1, the solution is Theta(n^p (1 + integral of g(u)/u^{p+1})), where sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1.
short: One exponent p captures arbitrarily uneven splits.
long: One exponent p captures arbitrarily uneven splits. It generalises the standard equal-split recurrence theorem to multiple unequal subproblems.
proof: A change of variables to logarithmic scale turns the recurrence into a renewal equation whose characteristic exponent is p.
consequence: It resolves recurrences from algorithms with unbalanced partition sizes.

title: Dynamic Programming Optimal Substructure
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem has optimal substructure when an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.
short: Optimal answers can be assembled from optimal smaller answers.
long: Optimal answers can be assembled from optimal smaller answers. It is one of the two hallmarks of dynamic programming, alongside overlapping subproblems.
proof: If a sub-solution could be improved while keeping the rest fixed, the whole solution would improve, contradicting optimality.
consequence: It justifies Bellman equations and bottom-up DP recurrences.

title: Memoisation versus Tabulation
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Memoisation caches results of recursive calls on demand, while tabulation fills a table bottom-up in dependency order.
short: Top-down caching versus bottom-up iteration.
long: Top-down caching versus bottom-up iteration. Both achieve one computation per distinct subproblem; tabulation avoids recursion overhead and controls space.
proof: Each memoised call computes a state once, as does each table entry filled in order.
consequence: The choice affects stack depth, cache behaviour and ease of state compression.

title: Overlapping Subproblems Criterion
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A recursive algorithm has overlapping subproblems when the same subproblem is solved repeatedly, making caching worthwhile.
short: DP wins when recursion re-solves the same work.
long: DP wins when recursion re-solves the same work. Quicksort has disjoint subproblems and gains nothing from memoisation; Fibonacci recursion has heavy overlap.
proof: If the recursion tree has repeated nodes, storing results replaces repeated subtrees by table lookups.
consequence: It distinguishes dynamic programming from ordinary divide and conquer.

title: Greedy Choice Property
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem has the greedy choice property if some optimal solution begins with the locally best choice.
short: A myopic first move can be provably safe.
long: A myopic first move can be provably safe. It must be established for each problem; greedy algorithms fail without it.
proof: An exchange argument transforms an optimal solution into one making the greedy choice without increasing cost.
consequence: It underlies Huffman coding, interval scheduling and MST algorithms.

title: Exchange Arguments for Greedy Correctness
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An exchange argument shows a greedy choice is safe by modifying any optimal solution to include it without worsening the objective.
short: Convert the best solution into one agreeing with greedy.
long: Convert the best solution into one agreeing with greedy. The technique appears in proofs of Kruskal, Prim, Huffman and interval scheduling.
proof: Locate the greedy element in the optimal solution's structure, swap it in and verify constraints and cost.
consequence: It is the workhorse proof technique for greedy optimality.

title: Matroid Greedy Optimality
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For a weighted matroid, sorting elements by decreasing weight and adding each feasible element yields a maximum-weight independent set.
short: Matroid axioms are exactly what greedy needs.
long: Matroid axioms are exactly what greedy needs. Graphic matroids explain why Kruskal works; partition matroids model scheduling constraints.
proof: The exchange axiom lets any optimal basis be transformed to include the greedy prefix by induction.
consequence: It gives a uniform proof of many seemingly unrelated greedy algorithms.

title: Greedy Fails for 0/1 Knapsack
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Picking items by value-to-weight ratio can be suboptimal when items cannot be split.
short: Indivisibility breaks the ratio argument.
long: Indivisibility breaks the ratio argument. With capacity 50 and items (10,60), (20,100) and (30,120), greedy by ratio takes the first two for 160, while the last two give 220.
proof: The ratio order fills capacity with high-density items but leaves unusable space; no exchange argument can force the optimal pair to be chosen.
consequence: Use dynamic programming for 0/1 knapsack and greedy only for the fractional version.

title: 0/1 Knapsack Dynamic Program
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For n items and integer capacity W, DP over items and capacity solves 0/1 knapsack in O(nW) time and O(W) space with a rolling array.
short: Decide each item once against every reachable capacity.
long: Decide each item once against every reachable capacity. The bound is pseudopolynomial because W is a number, not the count of input bits.
proof: After processing item i, dp[w] stores the best value using a subset of the first i items with weight at most w.
consequence: It is the standard pseudo-polynomial algorithm for a fundamental NP-hard problem.

title: Fractional Knapsack Greedy Ratio
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: When items are divisible, sorting by value per unit weight and taking as much as possible gives an optimal solution in O(n log n).
short: Spend capacity on the best value per pound first.
long: Spend capacity on the best value per pound first. The final item may be taken partially, which is precisely why greedy is valid here.
proof: If a cheaper-per-unit item is taken while a dearer one remains, swapping mass increases value until no such inversion exists.
consequence: It contrasts with the 0/1 case and illustrates when greedy is exact.

title: Longest Common Subsequence DP
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The length of the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths n and m follows from a recurrence that either matches the last characters or discards one, computable in O(nm) time.
short: Build the answer from prefixes of both strings.
long: Build the answer from prefixes of both strings. Space can be reduced to O(min(n,m)) if only the length is needed.
proof: If the last characters match they can be used, otherwise at least one last character is discarded; the recurrence considers both cases.
consequence: It is a canonical DP template with applications in diff tools and bioinformatics.

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication Order
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Choosing parenthesization of a matrix product by DP minimises scalar multiplications in O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.
short: Try every split point for every interval of matrices.
long: Try every split point for every interval of matrices. The number of possible parenthesizations is Catalan, so DP gives an exponential saving.
proof: The last multiplication splits the chain at some k, so an optimal solution combines optimal solutions of the two sides.
consequence: It is the textbook example of interval DP and optimal substructure.

title: Interval Scheduling Greedy Choice
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Sorting intervals by finish time and accepting each compatible one maximises the number of scheduled intervals in O(n log n) time.
short: Finishing early leaves the most room for the rest.
long: Finishing early leaves the most room for the rest. Weighted interval scheduling instead requires dynamic programming.
proof: The earliest-finishing interval can be part of some optimal schedule by exchange, after which the same argument applies to compatible intervals.
consequence: It is the simplest nontrivial greedy scheduling algorithm.

title: Huffman Coding Greedy Optimality
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols produces an optimal prefix code in O(n log n) time with a priority queue.
short: Give short codes to frequent symbols by merging rare ones first.
long: Give short codes to frequent symbols by merging rare ones first. The resulting tree minimises expected code length for the given frequencies.
proof: The two least frequent symbols can be made deepest siblings in some optimal tree, reducing the problem to a merged symbol.
consequence: It is the classic application of greedy algorithms and heaps to data compression.

title: Alpha-Beta Pruning in Game Trees
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Alpha-beta pruning skips branches that cannot affect the minimax decision, reducing explored nodes to about b^{d/2} with good move ordering.
short: Stop searching a branch once it cannot change the answer.
long: Stop searching a branch once it cannot change the answer. Without good ordering the improvement can vanish; the bound is for ideal ordering.
proof: Maintaining alpha and beta bounds at ancestors allows cutoffs when a child's value exceeds the current bound.
consequence: It roughly doubles the depth reachable by game-playing programs.

title: Competitive Analysis of Online Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An online algorithm is c-competitive if its cost is at most c times the optimal offline cost plus a constant for every request sequence.
short: Compare against an adversary that knows the whole future.
long: Compare against an adversary that knows the whole future. It is the standard performance measure for caching, paging and scheduling under uncertainty.
proof: The ratio is taken as the supremum over all admissible request sequences.
consequence: It provides guarantees when probabilistic input models are unavailable.

title: Adversary Arguments for Lower Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An adversary lower bound constructs inputs adaptively so that any algorithm must spend a certain number of operations before it can be correct.
short: Force the algorithm to inspect enough of the input.
long: Force the algorithm to inspect enough of the input. The unsorted-search bound and comparison-sort bound can both be phrased adversarially.
proof: The adversary keeps at least two consistent inputs indistinguishable until enough queries distinguish them.
consequence: It is a flexible tool for proving impossibility results.

title: Las Vegas versus Monte Carlo Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Las Vegas algorithms always give a correct answer with random running time, while Monte Carlo algorithms have bounded running time with a small probability of error.
short: Randomise the time or randomise the correctness.
long: Randomise the time or randomise the correctness. Randomised quicksort is Las Vegas; Rabin–Karp with a random modulus is Monte Carlo.
proof: The distinction follows from which of time and correctness is guaranteed with probability one.
consequence: It guides algorithm selection when failure probability matters.

title: Pseudopolynomial Time and Strong NP-Hardness
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An algorithm is pseudopolynomial if it is polynomial in numeric input values but not in the number of bits encoding them, as with O(nW) knapsack DP.
short: Large numbers encoded in few bits can break the bound.
long: Large numbers encoded in few bits can break the bound. A problem strongly NP-hard has no pseudopolynomial algorithm unless P = NP.
proof: W requires log W bits, so an algorithm linear in W is exponential in the input length.
consequence: It clarifies why some NP-hard problems admit practical DP while others do not.

title: NP-Hard versus NP-Complete
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it; it is NP-complete if it is also in NP.
short: NP-completeness adds verifiability to hardness.
long: NP-completeness adds verifiability to hardness. Optimisation problems such as TSP are typically NP-hard but not formally NP-complete.
proof: The definitions differ only in the membership requirement in NP.
consequence: It determines whether a problem can be certified quickly as well as being hard.

title: Polynomial-Time Reductions
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A polynomial-time many-one reduction maps instances of A to instances of B in polynomial time so that x is in A iff f(x) is in B.
short: Solving B efficiently would solve A efficiently.
long: Solving B efficiently would solve A efficiently. Reductions are the tool for transferring hardness and algorithms between problems.
proof: Composing an algorithm for B with the reduction yields an algorithm for A.
consequence: They define NP-hardness and structure the map of computational difficulty.

title: Fixed-Parameter Tractability
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem is fixed-parameter tractable with parameter k if it can be solved in f(k) poly(n) time for some computable f.
short: Confine exponential work to a small parameter.
long: Confine exponential work to a small parameter. Vertex cover is FPT with k the cover size; kernelisation and branching are standard techniques.
proof: An algorithm meeting the form is by definition FPT, independent of n in its exponential part.
consequence: It provides a positive algorithmic theory for problems that are NP-hard in general.

title: PSPACE and Space Complexity
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: PSPACE is the class of decision problems solvable with a polynomial amount of memory, regardless of running time.
short: Memory, not time, is the scarce resource.
long: Memory, not time, is the scarce resource. By Savitch's theorem, PSPACE equals NPSPACE up to a quadratic blow-up in space.
proof: The class is defined by Turing machines with polynomial space bounds.
consequence: It captures games and quantified formulas where time may be exponential.

title: Time-Space Tradeoffs in Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Many algorithms exchange memory for speed, as when a DP table gives O(1) lookup per state while a rolling array saves space but loses reconstructability.
short: Keeping more information usually speeds up queries.
long: Keeping more information usually speeds up queries. Hirschberg's algorithm recovers an LCS with linear space at the cost of extra recursive time.
proof: Storing intermediate results avoids recomputation, reducing time at the cost of memory cells.
consequence: Memory limits often dictate which algorithm variant is usable.

title: Information-Theoretic Lower Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: If an algorithm's answers distinguish N possible inputs, each yes/no query yields at most one bit, so at least log2 N queries are needed.
short: Count how many possibilities must be ruled out.
long: Count how many possibilities must be ruled out. This yields the log n bound for searching and the n log n bound for sorting permutations.
proof: A depth-d binary decision tree has at most 2^d leaves, so 2^d >= N implies d >= log2 N.
consequence: It turns counting arguments into rigorous impossibility results.

title: Ski Rental Competitive Ratio
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Buying skis after renting for exactly B days achieves competitive ratio 2 for the ski rental problem, and randomisation improves it to e/(e-1).
short: Wait until rentals would equal the purchase price.
long: Wait until rentals would equal the purchase price. It is the simplest benchmark problem in online decision making.
proof: If skiing stops before B days the cost matches OPT; otherwise rentals plus purchase are at most twice OPT.
consequence: It illustrates competitive analysis against an all-knowing offline optimum.

title: Work and Span of a Parallel Computation
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Work W is total operations and span S is the longest dependency chain; on p processors Brent's bound gives time at most W/p + S.
short: Divide work by processors, but dependencies set a floor.
long: Divide work by processors, but dependencies set a floor. Efficiency is W/(p T_p); a large span limits scalability.
proof: Greedy scheduling performs at most W/p work per step in parallel and cannot finish before the critical path S completes.
consequence: Work and span replace plain running time in parallel algorithm analysis.

title: Element Distinctness Lower Bound
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Deciding whether n real numbers are all distinct requires Omega(n log n) comparisons in the algebraic decision tree model.
short: Even yes/no uniqueness needs sorting-like work.
long: Even yes/no uniqueness needs sorting-like work. The bound motivated the algebraic decision tree model as a generalisation of comparison trees.
proof: The input space has Theta(n!) connected components corresponding to orderings, and each comparison tree leaf can cover only one.
consequence: Hashing gives expected linear time for discrete keys but not in the comparison model.

title: Concentration of Randomised Quicksort
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Randomised quicksort's running time is O(n log n) with high probability, not merely in expectation.
short: Bad pivot sequences are extremely unlikely.
long: Bad pivot sequences are extremely unlikely. Tail bounds follow from concentration of the number of comparisons, a sum of weakly dependent indicator variables.
proof: Azuma's inequality or bounded-differences arguments bound the deviation of comparison count from its expectation.
consequence: Randomised algorithms can offer robust probabilistic performance guarantees.

title: Smoothed Analysis of Algorithms
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Smoothed analysis measures running time on inputs obtained by slightly perturbing arbitrary instances, explaining why algorithms with bad worst cases often work well.
short: Between worst case and average case lies a realistic model.
long: Between worst case and average case lies a realistic model. The simplex method has polynomial smoothed complexity, in contrast to exponential worst-case examples.
proof: Perturbation limits how long an adversarial construction can survive, bounding the expected number of pivot steps.
consequence: It bridges theory and practice for numerics and local-search heuristics.

title: Iterated Square-Root Recurrence
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The recurrence T(n) = T(sqrt n) + O(1) solves to Theta(log log n).
short: Repeated square roots shrink n doubly exponentially fast.
long: Repeated square roots shrink n doubly exponentially fast. After k steps the argument is n^{1/2^k}, which becomes constant once k is about log2 log2 n.
proof: Set n_k = n^{1/2^k}; taking logs gives log n_k = (log n)/2^k, so k = log log n reaches a constant.
consequence: It appears in analysis of some union-find and integer algorithms.

title: Fenwick Tree Prefix Sum Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A Fenwick tree stores at index i the sum of the range (i - lowbit(i) + 1)..i, where lowbit(i) is the largest power of two dividing i.
short: Overlapping power-of-two blocks encode prefix sums.
long: Overlapping power-of-two blocks encode prefix sums. It uses a single array of size n and supports prefix sums in O(log n) time.
proof: Repeatedly subtracting lowbit(i) decomposes [1..i] into disjoint stored blocks.
consequence: Fenwick trees are a compact alternative to segment trees for prefix-sum workloads.

title: Fenwick Point Update and Prefix Query
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Adding delta at position i means adding it to bit[j] for j = i, i + lowbit(i), ...; querying the prefix sum walks j = i, i - lowbit(i), ...
short: Indices climb for updates and descend for queries.
long: Indices climb for updates and descend for queries. Both loops visit at most log2 n entries, and the tree is built in O(n log n) or O(n) by a direct pass.
proof: Each update changes exactly the stored blocks containing i, and each query sums exactly the blocks covering the prefix.
consequence: It is the standard dynamic cumulative-frequency structure.

title: Fenwick Range Sum by Difference of Prefixes
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A range sum on a Fenwick tree is prefix(r) - prefix(l-1), costing O(log n).
short: Two prefix queries give any interval.
long: Two prefix queries give any interval. Two Fenwick trees can instead support range updates with point queries in O(log n).
proof: Prefix sums are additive over the difference of the two index ranges.
consequence: It makes Fenwick trees usable for general range sum problems.

title: Fenwick versus Segment Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Fenwick trees are smaller and faster for invertible prefix aggregates such as sums, while segment trees support arbitrary associative operations and range updates on general intervals.
short: Specialised simplicity versus general flexibility.
long: Specialised simplicity versus general flexibility. Fenwick trees need an inverse operation to subtract prefixes; segment trees work for min, max and custom monoids.
proof: Fenwick blocks are fixed by index arithmetic; segment-tree nodes correspond to arbitrary intervals of the recursion.
consequence: Choose Fenwick for sums and frequencies, segment trees for min/max and lazy updates.

title: Segment Tree for Range Aggregation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A segment tree stores an associative aggregate for each dyadic interval of an array, with leaves holding single elements.
short: A balanced binary tree over array intervals.
long: A balanced binary tree over array intervals. It supports point updates and range queries in O(log n) time for any associative operation.
proof: Any query interval decomposes into O(log n) canonical tree nodes.
consequence: Segment trees generalise Fenwick trees to min, max, gcd and custom monoids.

title: Segment Tree Query and Update Bounds
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: With n leaves, a segment tree answers range queries and performs point updates in O(log n) time and uses O(n) space.
short: Tree height is logarithmic and queries touch few nodes.
long: Tree height is logarithmic and queries touch few nodes. An implicit heap layout uses at most 4n nodes.
proof: A range query visits at most two root-to-leaf paths plus their side branches; a point update follows one path.
consequence: The bounds make segment trees a workhorse of competitive and systems programming.

title: Lazy Propagation for Range Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Storing pending updates at covered segment-tree nodes and pushing them down only when needed supports range add and range sum in O(log n) per operation.
short: Defer work until a child is actually visited.
long: Defer work until a child is actually visited. Without laziness, a range update would touch O(k log n) elements explicitly.
proof: A range update marks O(log n) canonical nodes; the stored tags are applied during later traversals.
consequence: Lazy propagation extends segment trees to range-assignment and range-add workloads.

title: Linear-Time Segment Tree Construction
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Filling leaves and computing internal nodes bottom-up builds a segment tree in O(n) time.
short: One pass over internal nodes suffices.
long: One pass over internal nodes suffices. Repeated point updates would build the same tree in O(n log n).
proof: There are n-1 internal nodes, each computed in constant time from its two children.
consequence: Construction is never the bottleneck in segment-tree applications.

title: Persistent Segment Tree Versions
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Copying only the O(log n) nodes on a modified root-to-leaf path creates a new version of a segment tree in O(log n) time and space.
short: Path copying shares all untouched subtrees.
long: Path copying shares all untouched subtrees. Old versions remain queryable, enabling time-travel queries such as range k-th statistics over prefixes.
proof: Nodes outside the updated path are immutable and can be shared safely between versions.
consequence: Persistence adds historical queries at logarithmic overhead.

title: Sparse Dynamic Segment Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: When only a few positions of a huge coordinate range are set, allocating nodes lazily along update paths uses O(k log U) space for k updates in a universe U.
short: Do not materialise empty intervals.
long: Do not materialise empty intervals. It supports the same O(log U) operations as a full segment tree on sparse data.
proof: Each update creates at most one node per level of the coordinate tree.
consequence: Dynamic segment trees handle 64-bit coordinate spaces without allocating terabytes.

title: Two-Dimensional Fenwick Tree
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Nesting Fenwick trees over rows and columns supports point updates and rectangle-sum queries on an n by m grid in O(log n log m) time.
short: Apply the one-dimensional trick in both coordinates.
long: Apply the one-dimensional trick in both coordinates. Space is O(nm), and sparse maps can reduce it for large sparse grids.
proof: A rectangle sum is a combination of four 2D prefix sums, each computed with nested lowbit loops.
