consequence: 2D BITs are standard for offline counting and dynamic frequency grids.

title: Range Tree for Orthogonal Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A 2D range tree is a balanced tree on x-coordinates with each node storing a secondary sorted structure on the y-coordinates of its subtree.
short: A tree of sorted lists answers rectangle queries.
long: A tree of sorted lists answers rectangle queries. All points of a node's subtree are sorted by y for reporting points in an x-range and y-range.
proof: An x-range decomposes into O(log n) canonical nodes, each searched in its y-list.
consequence: Range trees solve orthogonal range reporting and counting in logarithmic-ish time.

title: Range Tree Query Complexity
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A 2D range tree reports k points in an orthogonal rectangle in O(log^2 n + k) time using O(n log n) space.
short: Logarithmic search at each of logarithmically many nodes.
long: Logarithmic search at each of logarithmically many nodes. In d dimensions the bound generalises to O(log^d n + k) with O(n log^{d-1} n) space.
proof: There are O(log n) canonical x-nodes and each secondary search costs O(log n) plus output.
consequence: It is the baseline for comparing specialised spatial indexes.

title: Fractional Cascading in Range Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Adding pointers between corresponding entries of sorted child lists reduces 2D range reporting to O(log n + k) time.
short: Reuse the search position from one list in the next.
long: Reuse the search position from one list in the next. The extra pointers increase space by a constant factor only.
proof: A binary search at the root yields candidate ranks that can be followed downward via cascade pointers in O(1) per level.
consequence: Fractional cascading removes one logarithmic factor from many multi-level searches.

title: Wavelet Tree Sequence Statistics
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A wavelet tree recursively partitions an alphabet, storing at each node a bitvector recording which branch each sequence element takes.
short: Binary search over the alphabet, with bitvectors per level.
long: Binary search over the alphabet, with bitvectors per level. It supports rank, select, access, quantile and range counting in O(log sigma) time.
proof: Each level halves the alphabet, so the tree has depth log sigma and bitvector ranks navigate it.
consequence: Wavelet trees provide compressed, fast indexes for strings and sequences.

title: Merge Sort Tree for Range Counting
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Storing the sorted list of each segment-tree node lets a range count values below x in O(log^2 n) time using O(n log n) space.
short: Segment tree nodes act as pre-sorted summaries.
long: Segment tree nodes act as pre-sorted summaries. Range k-th smallest can be found by binary searching the answer value with these counts.
proof: The query interval decomposes into O(log n) nodes and each binary search costs O(log n).
consequence: It is a simple static solution to range quantile and counting queries.

title: Mo's Algorithm for Offline Range Queries
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Sorting queries by block of left endpoint and then by right endpoint lets all q range queries on a static array be answered with O((n+q) sqrt n) pointer moves.
short: Reuse a sliding interval between similar queries.
long: Reuse a sliding interval between similar queries. It applies when queries can be reordered and the aggregate supports cheap add/remove of one element.
proof: Right endpoints move at most n times per left-block, and there are O(n/sqrt n) blocks, giving O(n sqrt n) moves.
consequence: It is a standard offline trick for range-distinct and range-mode problems.

title: Sqrt Decomposition Array Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Splitting an array into blocks of size about sqrt n supports range add by adjusting whole-block tags and point queries in O(sqrt n) time.
short: Coarse block summaries plus small boundary scans.
long: Coarse block summaries plus small boundary scans. It is easy to implement and often fast due to good constants.
proof: A range covers at most O(sqrt n) whole blocks and at most 2sqrt n boundary elements.
consequence: It provides a simple fallback where segment trees are overkill.

title: Link-Cut Tree Dynamic Forest Operations
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Link-cut trees represent dynamic forests and support link, cut, path aggregate and connectivity queries in O(log n) amortised time.
short: Represented paths as splay trees enable dynamic tree queries.
long: Represented paths as splay trees enable dynamic tree queries. They do not support general graph updates, only forests.
proof: Preferred paths are stored in splay trees, and splay operations rebalance after each access.
consequence: They enable dynamic network flows and online tree path queries.

title: Euler Tour Tree for Dynamic Connectivity
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Representing each tree by its Euler tour in a balanced BST supports link, cut and connectivity queries in O(log n) amortised time.
short: A tree becomes a sequence of directed edges.
long: A tree becomes a sequence of directed edges. Link and cut splice Euler-tour sequences; component membership is read from the represented tree.
proof: Rotations in the sequence correspond to rerooting, and balanced BST splits and merges take logarithmic time.
consequence: ET-trees are an alternative to link-cut trees for dynamic forests.

title: Heavy-Light Decomposition of Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Choosing the largest child as heavy decomposes any root-to-leaf path into O(log n) light-edge segments that map to contiguous array ranges.
short: Convert tree paths into a few array intervals.
long: Convert tree paths into a few array intervals. Each light edge at least halves subtree size, bounding their number on a path.
proof: Following a light edge moves into a subtree of at most half the size, so at most log n such edges occur.
consequence: It reduces path queries on a static tree to segment-tree range queries.

title: Link-Cut versus Heavy-Light Trade-off
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Heavy-light decomposition is simpler and gives deterministic O(log^2 n) path queries on static trees, while link-cut trees allow topology changes at amortised O(log n) cost.
short: Static simplicity versus dynamic flexibility.
long: Static simplicity versus dynamic flexibility. Link-cut trees have larger constants and more subtle invariants.
proof: Heavy-light relies on fixed subtree sizes; link-cut trees rebalance preferred paths dynamically.
consequence: Choose based on whether the underlying tree ever changes.

title: Disjoint Sparse Table for Static RMQ
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A disjoint sparse table answers idempotent static range queries in O(1) time with O(n log n) preprocessing and space.
short: Precompute suffixes and prefixes inside disjoint blocks.
long: Precompute suffixes and prefixes inside disjoint blocks. Unlike a standard sparse table, it handles overlapping queries of any length with two precomputed blocks.
proof: A range crossing a power-of-two boundary is covered by two precomputed half-block aggregates.
consequence: It is an alternative constant-time RMQ structure with simple preprocessing.

title: Sparse Tables Are Static Only
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Changing one array element invalidates Theta(n log n) sparse-table entries, so the structure cannot support efficient updates.
short: Constant-time queries come at the price of immutability.
long: Constant-time queries come at the price of immutability. Dynamic RMQ needs segment trees or Fischer–Heun style structures with different trade-offs.
proof: Each level of the sparse table stores overlapping blocks that all contain the updated index.
consequence: Check update requirements before choosing a static RMQ structure.

title: Persistent Balanced Search Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Path copying in an AVL or red-black tree produces a fully persistent ordered map with O(log n) time and space per update.
short: Immutable nodes let every version coexist.
long: Immutable nodes let every version coexist. Balance fields are recomputed on the copied path; rotation may create a constant number of extra nodes.
proof: Only nodes on the modified root-to-leaf path change, so sharing the rest preserves all invariants.
consequence: Persistent maps underpin functional collections and versioned databases.

title: Rollback Union-Find
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Recording parent and rank changes lets union-find undo the most recent unions, enabling divide-and-conquer and rollback-based offline algorithms.
short: Log changes and rewind when leaving a recursion branch.
long: Log changes and rewind when leaving a recursion branch. Path compression is usually disabled or carefully logged because it complicates rollback.
proof: Each union changes a constant number of fields, so a stack of changes suffices to restore prior state.
consequence: It is used in offline dynamic connectivity and segment-tree-over-time solutions.

title: Online Dynamic Connectivity with ET-Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Euler tour trees maintain connectivity under link and cut operations in an amortised O(log^2 n) per update in the worst case.
short: Balanced Euler tours support online topology changes.
long: Balanced Euler tours support online topology changes. Faster randomised and deterministic structures exist, but ET-trees are conceptually simple.
proof: Link and cut are split-and-merge operations on balanced BST sequences, with logarithmic overhead per structural change.
consequence: They handle connectivity when updates arrive without knowledge of the future.

title: LSM Tree Write Amplification
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: LSM trees absorb writes in an in-memory memtable and flush sorted runs, so a logical write may be physically written several times during compaction.
short: Cheap writes are paid for later by merging runs.
long: Cheap writes are paid for later by merging runs. Write amplification is the ratio of bytes written to storage to bytes written by the application.
proof: Each level merge rewrites existing data along with new data, multiplying physical writes.
consequence: Compaction policy trades write amplification against read and space amplification.

title: LSM Tree Read Path
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An LSM lookup checks the memtable and then successive on-disk levels, often using bloom filters to skip levels that cannot contain the key.
short: Newest data is checked first; filters prune older runs.
long: Newest data is checked first; filters prune older runs. Point lookups can touch many levels, while range scans merge iterators across runs.
proof: Each level is a sorted immutable run, so a binary search per level locates candidate entries.
consequence: Bloom filters are essential to keep point-read latency acceptable.

title: LSM Compaction Strategies
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Size-tiered compaction merges similarly sized runs to favour writes, while leveled compaction maintains one sorted level per size to favour reads.
short: Choose which amplification to minimise.
long: Choose which amplification to minimise. Leveled designs reduce read and space amplification at the cost of more write amplification.
proof: Merging runs of equal size rewrites each byte once per level in leveled designs, bounding overlap.
consequence: The choice dominates the behaviour of modern key-value stores.

title: B-epsilon Tree Write Optimisation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A B-epsilon tree puts buffers of size epsilon B at internal nodes so that inserts are batched before being pushed down, reducing insertion I/Os by a factor B^epsilon.
short: Buffer writes to amortise disk transfers.
long: Buffer writes to amortise disk transfers. Point queries must check buffers along the search path, increasing read cost relative to a B-tree.
proof: Each buffer flush sends epsilon B entries in one I/O, amortising the transfer across many inserts.
consequence: It is a write-optimised index for update-heavy workloads.

title: Buffer Tree for Batched Updates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A buffer tree attaches an I/O-sized buffer to each node of a B-tree so that batches of updates are pushed down in sorted order.
short: Sort inside the tree to avoid random I/O.
long: Sort inside the tree to avoid random I/O. It is a core technique in cache-oblivious and external-memory graph algorithms.
proof: When a buffer fills, its contents are sorted and distributed in one sequential scan of children.
consequence: Batched updates become dramatically cheaper on disk.

title: R-Tree Spatial Index
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An R-tree indexes spatial objects by enclosing them in minimum bounding rectangles arranged in a balanced tree.
short: Bounding boxes organise objects by location.
long: Bounding boxes organise objects by location. Overlapping rectangles can force a query to visit many branches, so worst-case query time is O(n).
proof: Each internal node groups nearby rectangles, and a window query descends only into overlapping boxes.
consequence: R-trees are the default spatial index in geographic databases.

title: Bounding Volume Hierarchy
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A BVH recursively groups geometric objects into bounding volumes so ray intersection tests prune most of the scene.
short: Skip whole subtrees whose bounding volume misses the ray.
long: Skip whole subtrees whose bounding volume misses the ray. Quality depends on how tightly volumes bound their children and on split heuristics.
proof: A ray must intersect a node's volume before descending into its children.
consequence: BVHs are fundamental to ray tracing and collision detection.

title: Misra-Gries Heavy Hitters Summary
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: Keeping k-1 counters and decrementing all on a miss identifies every item with frequency exceeding n/k in one pass with O(k) space.
short: Repeated cancellation preserves frequent items.
long: Repeated cancellation preserves frequent items. Estimated counts may overestimate true counts but never underestimate them.
proof: Each decrement removes k distinct items, so a true heavy hitter cannot be eliminated completely.
consequence: It is the classic streaming heavy-hitters algorithm.

title: Count-Min Sketch Point Estimates
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A count-min sketch uses d hash functions into arrays of width w and reports the minimum of the d counters, never underestimating a frequency.
short: Hash collisions only inflate estimates.
long: Hash collisions only inflate estimates. Setting w = O(1/epsilon) and d = O(log(1/delta)) gives the standard guarantee.
proof: Collisions with the queried item are bounded by Markov's inequality and independent across rows.
consequence: It estimates frequencies in small space for streams and networking.

title: HyperLogLog Cardinality Estimation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct stream elements from the maximum number of leading zeros in hashed values across m registers.
short: Rare long runs of zeros reveal the cardinality.
long: Rare long runs of zeros reveal the cardinality. Space is O(m) registers, and a harmonic-mean correction removes bias.
proof: The probability that an item hashes to a value with k leading zeros is 2^{-k}, so the observed maximum estimates log n.
consequence: It estimates huge cardinalities with kilobytes of memory.

title: Quotient Filter Space Efficiency
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A quotient filter stores fingerprints in a hash-table-like array using quotienting, storing only the remainder bits and using the quotient as the bucket address.
short: Hash value doubles as the bucket address.
long: Hash value doubles as the bucket address. It supports insertions, lookups and deletions with locality better than a Bloom filter.
proof: Writing a fingerprint as quotient plus remainder lets the quotient be implicit in its array position.
consequence: It is a compact alternative to Bloom filters for large approximate sets.

title: Cuckoo Filter with Fingerprints
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A cuckoo filter stores short fingerprints in two candidate buckets derived from the key, supporting O(1) lookups and deletions with a small false positive rate.
short: Cuckoo hashing without storing full keys.
long: Cuckoo hashing without storing full keys. False positives arise from fingerprint collisions, so longer fingerprints reduce them at extra space cost.
proof: The two candidate buckets are computed from the key hash and its XOR with the fingerprint hash.
consequence: It gives a deletable, cache-friendly approximate membership structure.

title: Succinct Balanced-Parentheses Trees
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: An ordered rooted tree can be encoded in 2n + o(n) bits as a balanced-parentheses sequence supporting navigation in O(1) time.
short: Tree shape needs only two bits per node.
long: Tree shape needs only two bits per node. Rank and select on the bitstring implement parent, child and subtree-size queries.
proof: An open parenthesis denotes descent to a child and a close parenthesis denotes return to the parent.
consequence: Succinct trees compress large XML, DOM and ontology structures without losing access speed.

title: Succinct Graph Representation
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A dense undirected graph on n vertices can be stored in n^2 + o(n^2) bits while supporting degree and neighbour queries in constant time.
short: Store the adjacency matrix as bits plus a small index.
long: Store the adjacency matrix as bits plus a small index. Sparse graphs admit o(n^2) bit representations using degree-sorted adjacency lists.
proof: One bit per ordered pair encodes adjacency, and rank/select tables support neighbour enumeration.
consequence: Succinct graph encoding allows large graphs to reside in main memory.

title: Fusion Tree Word-RAM Searching
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A fusion tree searches n w-bit keys in O(log_w n) time by comparing several key bits in one word operation.
short: Pack a whole B-tree node's branching into a word.
long: Pack a whole B-tree node's branching into a word. With w >= log n this improves on the log n comparison bound, at the cost of complex bit manipulation.
proof: Sketching keys to O(log n) significant bits and using a fusion node finds the predecessor among up to w keys in constant time.
consequence: It shows how word-level parallelism breaks comparison-model lower bounds.

title: SWAR Broadword Parallelism
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: SWAR (SIMD within a register) packs several small fields into one machine word so that a single instruction updates all of them.
short: Arithmetic on subwords gives free parallelism.
long: Arithmetic on subwords gives free parallelism. Careful masks prevent carries from crossing field boundaries.
proof: Bitwise AND with repeated masks isolates each field, and one addition updates all fields simultaneously.
consequence: It accelerates bitvectors, succinct structures and small-integer arrays.

title: Retroactive Data Structures
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A retroactive data structure supports updates in the past and queries at arbitrary historical times, rather than only appending new versions.
short: Edit history, not just append to it.
long: Edit history, not just append to it. Partially retroactive structures only allow past updates, while fully retroactive ones also allow past queries.
proof: Operations are stored in a timeline structure and local rebuilding repairs invariants around the modified point.
consequence: They model time-travel debugging and historical database queries.

title: Persistent Array by Path Copying
subject: Advanced Data Structures
statement: A balanced array with path copying supports read and write on any past version in O(log n) time and space.
short: A trie-like tree of chunks lets versions share unchanged blocks.
long: A trie-like tree of chunks lets versions share unchanged blocks. Chunk size is chosen to balance tree depth against copying cost.
proof: A write replaces only the leaf chunk and the log n nodes on its path, leaving all other chunks shared.
consequence: It generalises persistent stacks to random-access arrays.

title: PRAM Shared-Memory Parallel Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: The PRAM model has p synchronous processors sharing a common memory, running in lockstep with unit-time arithmetic and memory operations.
short: An idealised shared-memory parallel computer.
long: An idealised shared-memory parallel computer. Variants differ in whether concurrent reads or writes are allowed; analyse by work and depth.
proof: The model is an abstraction: each processor executes one instruction per step on its local data or shared memory.
consequence: It gives a clean setting for designing parallel algorithms before mapping to real hardware.

title: PRAM Concurrency Variants
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: EREW forbids concurrent reads and writes, CREW allows concurrent reads, and CRCW additionally allows concurrent writes resolved by common, arbitrary or priority rules.
short: Concurrency rules define the machine's power.
long: Concurrency rules define the machine's power. Algorithms designed for EREW are portable; CRCW can be more powerful for tasks such as leader election.
proof: Each model is a restriction or extension of the previous one's permitted memory-access patterns.
consequence: State the assumed variant when quoting PRAM running times.

title: Parallel Prefix Scan
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: An associative parallel prefix computes all running aggregates of n values in O(log n) depth and O(n) work.
short: Up-sweep and down-sweep compute all prefixes at once.
long: Up-sweep and down-sweep compute all prefixes at once. Scan is the parallel analogue of prefix sums and underlies sorting, compaction and recurrence solvers.
proof: A balanced reduction tree computes partial aggregates; a downward pass distributes carried prefixes to siblings.
consequence: Work-efficient scans are a core primitive of parallel algorithms.

title: Parallel Reduce and Map Patterns
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Map applies a function independently to all inputs and reduce combines them with an associative operator, giving O(log n) depth with O(n) work.
short: Independent mapping plus a reduction tree.
long: Independent mapping plus a reduction tree. These patterns are the building blocks of GPU and data-parallel frameworks.
proof: Mapping is embarrassingly parallel and reduction is a binary tree of associative operations.
consequence: They express many algorithms without explicit synchronisation.

title: Cole's Parallel Merge Sort Depth
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Cole's parallel merge sort sorts n keys on an EREW PRAM in O(log n) time using O(n log n) work.
short: Pipelining merges removes a logarithmic factor from depth.
long: Pipelining merges removes a logarithmic factor from depth. Naive parallel merge sort has O(log^2 n) depth; Cole's chained decomposition improves it.
proof: Dividing merges into small pipelined blocks allows each level to start before the previous one finishes while keeping work linearithmic.
consequence: It shows comparison sorting has logarithmic parallel depth with near-optimal work.

title: Parallel BFS Frontier Expansion
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Breadth-first search can process each layer in parallel by relaxing all outgoing edges of the current frontier, taking O(D) depth and O(V+E) work.
short: All vertices in a layer expand simultaneously.
long: All vertices in a layer expand simultaneously. Duplicate discoveries must be resolved atomically; low-diameter graphs expose the most parallelism.
proof: Layers are independent because edges within a layer cannot shorten distances to the next layer in an unweighted graph.
consequence: It is the standard parallel graph-traversal primitive.

title: MapReduce Programming Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: MapReduce processes data with a map function producing key-value pairs, a shuffle that groups pairs by key, and a reduce function aggregating each group.
short: Group by key, then aggregate.
long: Group by key, then aggregate. The framework handles parallelism, fault tolerance and data distribution.
proof: All records with the same key are routed to the same reducer, so reductions are independent.
consequence: It made large-scale batch data processing accessible to ordinary programmers.

title: MapReduce Sorting with Range Partitioners
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sampling the key distribution to choose partition boundaries lets MapReduce sort records with balanced reducer loads and local sorting at each reducer.
short: Partition by sampled ranges, then sort locally.
long: Partition by sampled ranges, then sort locally. Each reducer receives a contiguous key range, so concatenating reducer outputs yields a globally sorted file.
proof: Sample-based quantiles approximate equal-sized partitions, and local sorting preserves order within each range.
consequence: It is how production systems sort datasets far larger than one machine's memory.

title: MapReduce Join by Key
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A equi-join of two datasets can be implemented by mapping each record to its join key and reducing over the grouped pairs.
short: Matching keys meet at the same reducer.
long: Matching keys meet at the same reducer. Skew in key frequencies can overload one reducer, requiring skew-handling techniques.
proof: Every output pair agrees on its key, and all such pairs are co-located by the shuffle.
consequence: It is a fundamental large-scale database primitive.

title: Bulk Synchronous Parallel Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: BSP computes in supersteps: local computation, message sending, then a global barrier before the next superstep.
short: Compute, communicate, synchronise, repeat.
long: Compute, communicate, synchronise, repeat. Parameters are computation cost w, communication cost h times network gap g, and synchronization period L.
proof: The model charges each superstep for its slowest processor plus communication and barrier costs.
consequence: It gives predictable performance on distributed-memory machines.

title: Randomised Work Stealing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In work stealing, each processor keeps a deque of ready tasks and an idle processor steals from the opposite end of another processor's deque.
short: Thieves take old work; owners take new work.
long: Thieves take old work; owners take new work. Random victim choice gives good expected load balance with little communication.
proof: Classic randomized analyses bound the expected execution time in terms of total work T1 and critical-path length T-infinity.
consequence: Work stealing is used in Cilk, Java fork-join and many task runtimes.

title: Amdahl's Law for Speedup
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: If a fraction f of computation is inherently serial, the maximum speedup with p processors is at most 1/(f + (1-f)/p).
short: The serial fraction caps all speedup.
long: The serial fraction caps all speedup. As p grows the speedup approaches 1/f, no matter how many processors are added.
proof: Scaled time is fT + (1-f)T/p, so the ratio of original to scaled time gives the formula.
consequence: It warns that optimising only the parallel portion has diminishing returns.

title: Gustafson's Scaled Speedup
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: When problem size grows with the number of processors, scaled speedup can remain near-linear despite a fixed serial fraction.
short: Bigger machines tackle bigger problems.
long: Bigger machines tackle bigger problems. It offers a more optimistic complement to Amdahl's fixed-work view.
proof: Writing serial and parallel portions as fractions alpha and 1-alpha of the scaled run gives the linear expression.
consequence: It explains strong scaling results in scientific computing.

title: Race Conditions Break Determinism
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Two processes incrementing the same shared counter without synchronisation can lose updates, giving a nondeterministic result.
short: Read-modify-write needs mutual exclusion.
long: Read-modify-write needs mutual exclusion. The same program may produce different outputs on different schedules.
proof: Both processors can read the same old value before either writes, so one increment is lost.
consequence: Parallel algorithms must specify disjoint writes or use atomic operations and reductions.

title: Barrier Synchronization
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A barrier makes all participating threads wait until every thread reaches it before any proceeds.
short: A rendezvous point for parallel phases.
long: A rendezvous point for parallel phases. Tree and centralised barriers trade latency against contention; misuse can cause deadlock.
proof: No thread passes until the count of arrivals equals the number of participants.
consequence: Barriers separate phases in BSP and data-parallel loops.

title: Simulating PRAM on Interconnection Networks
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Any PRAM algorithm can be simulated on a suitably connected network with only a logarithmic slowdown using routing and hashing techniques.
short: Distributed memory need not lose much theoretical power.
long: Distributed memory need not lose much theoretical power. Constant-degree networks such as hypercubes and butterflies support such simulations.
proof: Emulate shared cells by distributing them across processors and routing each request in O(log p) steps.
consequence: PRAM bounds remain a useful first approximation on real networks.

title: Hypercube Network Diameter
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A d-dimensional hypercube with 2^d nodes has diameter d = log2 p, so any two processors communicate in at most log p routing steps.
short: Flip differing bits to route.
long: Flip differing bits to route. Each node has degree d, giving a good balance between connectivity and hardware cost.
proof: Flipping the differing bit positions one at a time transforms any node label into any other in Hamming distance steps.
consequence: Hypercubes were an early parallel-machine topology.

title: Butterfly Network Routing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A butterfly network routes any input to any output through log p stages using bit-fixing routes.
short: Each stage fixes one address bit.
long: Each stage fixes one address bit. It supports efficient emulation of shared memory and fast Fourier-style communication patterns.
proof: At stage i, route straight or cross according to bit i of source and destination until all bits match.
consequence: Butterflies underpin many parallel routing and sorting architectures.

title: External Memory Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: The external memory model has a fast memory of M items and disk blocks of B items, counting only block transfers as I/Os.
short: Optimise disk transfers, not CPU instructions.
long: Optimise disk transfers, not CPU instructions. Sequential scans cost Theta(N/B) I/Os; random access may cost one I/O per access.
proof: The model is a definition: computation is free while each block transfer costs one I/O.
consequence: It explains why B-trees and merge sort dominate disk-based systems.

title: External Sorting Lower Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sorting N items in external memory requires Theta((N/B) log_{M/B}(N/B)) I/Os under the standard tall-cache assumption.
short: Merge logarithmically many runs of size M/B blocks.
long: Merge logarithmically many runs of size M/B blocks. The bound is the external analogue of the comparison-sort lower bound.
proof: Each merge pass reads and writes the whole dataset once, and the number of passes is logarithmic in N/M.
consequence: It sets the target for external and cache-oblivious sorting algorithms.

title: External Merge Sort with Run Merging
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: External merge sort reads chunks of M items, sorts them in memory into runs, then merges runs using one input buffer per run and one output buffer.
short: Sort in memory, merge sequentially on disk.
long: Sort in memory, merge sequentially on disk. Multiway merging reduces the number of passes compared with binary merging.
proof: Each merge pass scans each item once in and once out, giving O(N/B) I/Os per pass and O(log_{M/B}(N/B)) passes.
consequence: It is the standard algorithm for sorting data larger than RAM.

title: B-Tree Search I/O Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A B-tree with fan-out Theta(B) searches N items in O(log_B N) block transfers.
short: Each level of the tree costs one disk read.
long: Each level of the tree costs one disk read. This is optimal for comparison-based external search.
proof: Each node fits in one block and has Theta(B) children, so height is logarithmic base B.
consequence: B-trees minimise disk I/O in database indexes.

title: Cache-Oblivious Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In the cache-oblivious model algorithms are written without knowing B or M yet achieve optimal I/O bounds on every block size.
short: Write once, optimal on every cache level.
long: Write once, optimal on every cache level. It uses an ideal fully associative cache with optimal replacement.
proof: Recursive divide-and-conquer layouts work across all scales, so no parameter tuning is needed.
consequence: A single algorithm can exploit an entire memory hierarchy automatically.

title: Cache-Oblivious Matrix Transpose
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Recursive quadrant-wise transposition achieves Theta(N^2/B) cache misses without knowing the block size.
short: Divide the matrix until blocks fit in cache.
long: Divide the matrix until blocks fit in cache. The recursion also respects multiple cache levels simultaneously.
proof: Once submatrices fit in cache the transfer is optimal; larger cases reduce to four recursive transposes.
consequence: It outperforms naive row-by-row transpose on large matrices.

title: Cache-Oblivious Sorting Bound
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Cache-oblivious sorting achieves O((N/B) log_{M/B}(N/B)) I/Os without knowing B or M.
short: Recursive distribution matches external merge sort.
long: Recursive distribution matches external merge sort. The funnelsort algorithm uses buffered merging to obtain the optimal bound.
proof: Recursive splitting until subproblems fit in cache, combined with buffer trees, yields the external-sort I/O bound at every level.
consequence: It gives one sorting routine optimal across all cache levels.

title: Cache-Oblivious B-Tree
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: A cache-oblivious B-tree supports searches and updates in O(log_B N) I/Os without knowing B, using a static binary tree laid out in van Emde Boas order.
short: Recursive layout simulates high fan-out at every block size.
long: Recursive layout simulates high fan-out at every block size. Updates use buffered rebuilds to maintain the layout efficiently.
proof: The vEB layout groups subtrees of the right height into contiguous blocks, so each memory level sees an effective B-tree.
consequence: It delivers B-tree I/O performance with no tuning parameters.

title: Streaming Model One-Pass Constraint
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In the streaming model data arrives as a long sequence and the algorithm uses sublinear memory with one or few passes.
short: See each item once, remember little.
long: See each item once, remember little. Exact answers are often impossible, so approximations and sketches are standard.
proof: The model restricts both memory and pass count, forcing summarisation.
consequence: It models routers, sensor networks and clickstream analysis.

title: Turnstile Stream Model
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: In a turnstile stream, items can be both inserted and deleted, so the underlying frequency vector receives positive and negative updates.
short: Frequencies can go down as well as up.
long: Frequencies can go down as well as up. Algorithms such as count-min sketches tolerate negative updates, while many heavy-hitters methods do not.
proof: The stream is modelled as a sequence of signed updates to a vector.
consequence: It captures network flows and dynamic multisets more realistically than insertion-only streams.

title: Reservoir Sampling Uniform Sample
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Keeping the j-th item with probability k/j replaces a uniformly chosen member of a size-k reservoir, yielding a uniform sample of any prefix of the stream.
short: Sample without knowing the stream length.
long: Sample without knowing the stream length. It uses one pass and O(k) memory.
proof: Induction: after j items each of them is in the reservoir with probability k/j.
consequence: It is the standard way to sample from huge or unknown-size datasets.

title: I/O Optimal Scanning and Hashing
subject: Parallel & External Algorithms
statement: Sequential scans are optimal in external memory, taking Theta(N/B) I/Os, whereas hash-table lookups can cost one I/O each.
short: Batching random accesses into sequential ones pays off.
long: Batching random accesses into sequential ones pays off. External hash tables arrange buckets so that probes within a bucket are contiguous.
proof: A scan transfers each block once; random accesses may touch a different block per item.
consequence: Disk-based systems prefer log-structured and sorted layouts over pointer-heavy structures.

title: KMP Prefix Function Definition
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The prefix function pi[i] of a string is the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of s[0..i].
short: Each position remembers its longest border.
long: Each position remembers its longest border. The whole function is computed in O(m) time for a pattern of length m.
proof: If pi[i-1] = k, only borders of the prefix of length k need checking when extending by one character.
consequence: It is the core table of the Knuth–Morris–Pratt matcher.

title: KMP Linear-Time Pattern Matching
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Using the prefix function to shift the pattern after a mismatch finds all occurrences in a text of length n in O(n + m) time.
short: Mismatches redirect via previously computed borders.
long: Mismatches redirect via previously computed borders. The text pointer never moves backward, so the bound is worst-case rather than average-case.
proof: Each text character is compared O(1) times amortised because every mismatch follows a failure link to a strictly shorter border.
consequence: KMP avoids the quadratic behaviour of naive matching on repetitive texts.

title: KMP Failure Links Avoid Text Backtracking
subject: String Algorithms
statement: After a mismatch, KMP shifts the pattern so that its longest matching prefix aligns with the text suffix, without re-examining text characters.
short: Reuse what already matched.
long: Reuse what already matched. This is what distinguishes KMP from naive backtracking matchers.
proof: Any shorter shift would misalign characters already known to match at the suffix.
consequence: It gives predictable linear performance on adversarial inputs.

title: Z-Function Longest Common Prefixes
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The Z-value at position i is the length of the longest common prefix of the whole string and the suffix starting at i.
short: Z-values measure self-similarity at every shift.
long: Z-values measure self-similarity at every shift. Z[0] is usually defined as 0 or n by convention.
proof: The definition is a direct comparison of the string with each of its suffixes.
consequence: Z-values support linear-time pattern matching and periodicity tests.

title: Z-Algorithm Linear Construction
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Maintaining the rightmost matching Z-box lets all Z-values of a string be computed in O(n) time.
short: Reuse inside previously matched intervals.
long: Reuse inside previously matched intervals. Combining pattern, separator and text with Z-values gives another linear pattern matcher.
proof: Comparisons inside an existing box are copied, and each comparison extending the box increases its right boundary.
consequence: The Z-algorithm is a compact alternative to the prefix function.

title: Rabin–Karp Rolling Hash
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Rabin–Karp slides a fixed-length window by removing the leading character's contribution and appending the new one, updating the hash in O(1) per shift.
short: Update the window hash instead of recomputing it.
long: Update the window hash instead of recomputing it. With verification of candidate matches the expected running time is O(n+m); a worst-case collision-rich input can be slower.
proof: Treating the window as a base-b polynomial, removal and appending are O(1) modular operations.
consequence: Rolling hashes enable multi-pattern search and plagiarism detection.

title: Rabin–Karp Expected versus Worst Case
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Rabin–Karp has expected O(n+m) time under random hashing but O(nm) worst case if an adversary forces hash collisions at every alignment.
short: Verification fixes correctness, not the collision count.
long: Verification fixes correctness, not the collision count. Using a large random prime makes adversarial collisions unlikely.
proof: Each of n alignments can in the worst case produce a collision requiring an O(m) string comparison.
consequence: It is a Monte Carlo style speed-up unless collisions are fully eliminated.

title: Hash Collisions Are Inevitable
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Any hash function mapping the infinite set of strings into finitely many hash values must collide on two different strings.
short: Pigeonhole principle forbids collision-free hashing.
long: Pigeonhole principle forbids collision-free hashing. Therefore every hash-based string algorithm needs either verification or an explicit collision probability bound.
proof: There are infinitely many strings and only 2^k possible k-bit hash values, so some value has multiple preimages.
consequence: Hash-based searches trade a small collision risk for speed.

title: Boyer–Moore Bad Character Rule
subject: String Algorithms
statement: On a mismatch the bad-character rule slides the pattern so that the mismatching text character aligns with its last occurrence in the pattern.
short: Jump past text characters the pattern cannot match.
long: Jump past text characters the pattern cannot match. Used alone it can still degrade to O(nm) on repetitive text.
proof: Any alignment placing a different pattern character opposite c cannot match, so those alignments are skipped safely.
consequence: It gives large average-case jumps for long patterns and large alphabets.

title: Boyer–Moore Good Suffix Rule
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The good-suffix rule shifts a pattern after a mismatch so that the matched suffix realigns with its next occurrence or with a matching prefix.
short: Use the matched tail to choose a safe jump.
long: Use the matched tail to choose a safe jump. Combined with the bad-character rule it is the classic Boyer–Moore algorithm; Galil's rule restores O(n+m) worst case.
proof: Any smaller shift would place a pattern substring inconsistent with the characters already matched.
consequence: Good-suffix preprocessing makes Boyer–Moore very fast in practice.

title: Boyer–Moore Sublinear Comparisons
subject: String Algorithms
statement: On long patterns and realistic text, Boyer–Moore can inspect only O(n/m) character alignments, far fewer than the text length.
short: Scan right to left and skip large blocks.
long: Scan right to left and skip large blocks. This is a best-case or average statement; worst-case safeguards require Galil's rule.
proof: Right-to-left matching usually fails early, and each failure shifts the pattern by close to its full length.
consequence: It is a classic example of an algorithm whose practical behaviour beats its naive worst-case picture.

title: Horspool Simplified Bad-Character Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Horspool's algorithm compares right to left but always shifts by the last-character bad-character table, avoiding good-suffix preprocessing.
short: One shift table is often enough in practice.
long: One shift table is often enough in practice. It is a simplification of Boyer–Moore with competitive real-world speed.
proof: The shift table computed from the pattern's last character gives a safe alignment after each mismatch.
consequence: It is a popular lightweight substring-search routine.

title: Aho–Corasick Multiple-Pattern Automaton
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Aho–Corasick builds a trie of patterns augmented with failure links, finding all occurrences of all patterns in a text in one pass.
short: A trie with failure links is a finite-state matcher.
long: A trie with failure links is a finite-state matcher. m is the total length of all patterns.
proof: Failure links lead to the longest proper suffix that is a trie prefix, so each text character advances the state at most once amortised.
consequence: It is the standard solution for keyword filtering and intrusion detection.

title: Aho–Corasick Output Links
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Propagating output links through failure chains reports every pattern ending at a state in time proportional to the number of reports.
short: Inherit matches from suffix states.
long: Inherit matches from suffix states. Without output links, reporting all matches could cost time proportional to the number of patterns per text position.
proof: A pattern ending at a suffix of the current string is stored along the failure chain, so each report is traversed once.
consequence: It makes multi-pattern matching output-sensitive.

title: Suffix Tree Compresses All Suffixes
subject: String Algorithms
statement: A suffix tree is a compressed trie of all suffixes of a string, using O(n) nodes and supporting substring searches in O(m) time.
short: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix.
long: Every substring is a prefix of some suffix. Edges are labelled by substrings, and compressed paths eliminate unary nodes.
proof: A compressed trie of n suffixes has at most 2n nodes because leaves number n and internal nodes have at least two children.
consequence: Suffix trees answer many string queries in linear or near-linear time.

title: Suffix Array Definition
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The suffix array of a string lists the starting positions of all suffixes in lexicographic order.
short: A sorted list of suffixes replaces a tree.
long: A sorted list of suffixes replaces a tree. It uses O(n) space and, with an LCP array, supports many suffix-tree-like queries.
proof: Sorting suffixes is equivalent to sorting all substrings that extend to the end of the string.
consequence: Suffix arrays are simpler and more compact than suffix trees in practice.

title: Suffix Array Doubling Construction
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Doubling sorts suffixes by their first 2^k characters using rank pairs and counting sort, constructing the suffix array in O(n log n) time.
short: Sort by length-2 substrings, then double repeatedly.
long: Sort by length-2 substrings, then double repeatedly. SA-IS improves this to O(n) time for constant alphabets.
proof: The ranks for length 2^k determine the ranks for length 2^{k+1} via lexicographic order of rank pairs.
consequence: It is the standard implementable suffix-array construction.

title: Suffix Tree from Suffix Array and LCP
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The LCP array of adjacent suffixes together with the suffix array determines the suffix-tree topology.
short: LCP values give internal-node depths.
long: LCP values give internal-node depths. A stack-based scan of the LCP array builds the tree in linear time.
proof: Adjacent suffixes in suffix-array order share deepest prefixes given by LCP values, matching tree internal nodes.
consequence: It lets implementations enjoy suffix-array compactness and suffix-tree power.

title: Ukkonen's Online Suffix Tree
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Ukkonen's algorithm builds a suffix tree left to right in O(n) time for constant alphabets.
short: Extend all suffixes incrementally with suffix links.
long: Extend all suffixes incrementally with suffix links. It is online: each prefix's tree is valid before reading the next character.
proof: An active point tracks the current insertion position and suffix links jump between related nodes, bounding total work.
consequence: It is the classic linear-time suffix-tree construction.

title: Kasai's LCP Array Algorithm
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Scanning suffixes in text order while carrying the current match length computes the LCP array in O(n) time.
short: Adjacent suffixes in text order can reuse the previous comparison length.
long: Adjacent suffixes in text order can reuse the previous comparison length. Decrementing the carried value by one per position keeps total comparisons linear.
proof: If suffixes at i-1 and j share l characters, suffixes at i and j+1 share at least l-1.
consequence: It turns an O(n log n) or quadratic LCP computation into linear time.

title: LCP Array and Longest Repeated Substring
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The maximum entry of the LCP array is the length of the longest substring appearing at least twice in the string.
short: Adjacent suffixes in sorted order share the longest repeats.
long: Adjacent suffixes in sorted order share the longest repeats. Any repeated substring appears as a prefix of two suffixes whose LCP is at least its length.
proof: The two suffixes with a common repeated prefix occupy positions in the suffix array with all intervening LCP values at least that length, so the maximum captures it.
consequence: It gives a linear-time longest-repeat query after suffix-array construction.

title: Burrows–Wheeler Transform
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The BWT sorts all rotations of a string and writes the last column of the resulting matrix, often grouping repeated characters into long runs.
short: Reorder characters to improve compressibility.
long: Reorder characters to improve compressibility. It is invertible when the original string ends with a unique sentinel character.
proof: Sorting rotations creates rows whose last characters correspond to preceding characters in the original text.
consequence: It underpins bzip2 and modern genomic compressors.

title: BWT Invertibility via LF Mapping
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The k-th occurrence of a character in the last BWT column corresponds to the k-th occurrence in the first column, allowing the original string to be reconstructed.
short: Occurrence ranks link last and first columns.
long: Occurrence ranks link last and first columns. Repeated LF steps trace the text backwards from the sentinel.
proof: Sorting rotations preserves the relative order of equal-character rows, so occurrence ranks match across columns.
consequence: LF mapping enables both inversion and suffix-array-free text searches.

title: FM-Index Substring Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The FM-index searches a pattern backwards in the BWT by maintaining a suffix-array interval and updating it with rank queries.
short: Extend matches one character at a time using BWT ranks.
long: Extend matches one character at a time using BWT ranks. It provides compressed full-text search with space close to the compressed text.
proof: The interval of suffixes prefixed by cP is obtained from the interval for P by applying LF mapping restricted to c.
consequence: It is foundational for genomic short-read alignment.

title: Suffix Automaton States
subject: String Algorithms
statement: The suffix automaton of a string is a minimal DFA accepting all its substrings, with at most 2n-1 states for a string of length n.
short: A compact automaton for every substring.
long: A compact automaton for every substring. It can be built online in O(n) time for constant alphabets.
proof: Each extension creates at most one new state, and cloning splits at most one existing state.
consequence: It supports substring counting and longest-common-substring queries efficiently.

title: Levenshtein Edit Distance DP
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Edit distance with insertions, deletions and substitutions of cost 1 is computed by DP in O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space.
short: Fill a grid of prefix-to-prefix costs.
long: Fill a grid of prefix-to-prefix costs. If characters match, the diagonal value is inherited at no cost.
proof: The last operation in an optimal alignment must be one of the three edits handled by the recurrence.
consequence: It is the standard measure for spell-checking and sequence comparison.

title: Damerau–Levenshtein Transpositions
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Damerau–Levenshtein distance additionally allows swapping two adjacent characters as a single edit.
short: Adjacent typos cost one edit, not two.
long: Adjacent typos cost one edit, not two. The optimal string alignment variant forbids overlapping transpositions and is computed by the simple four-case recurrence.
proof: Adding a transposition case to the standard edit-distance recurrence handles swapped adjacent characters.
consequence: It improves spell-checking accuracy for common keyboard errors.

title: Hirschberg Linear-Space LCS
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Hirschberg's algorithm computes an actual longest common subsequence in O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space by divide and conquer over rows.
short: Recompute forward and backward DP at the split row.
long: Recompute forward and backward DP at the split row. It retains the standard LCS time bound while eliminating the quadratic table.
proof: A middle row from forward and backward passes identifies the optimal split point, after which the two halves are solved recursively.
consequence: It makes LCS feasible for long sequences with limited memory.

title: Manacher's Linear Palindrome Search
subject: String Algorithms
statement: Manacher's algorithm finds the longest palindromic substring centred at every position in O(n) time by reusing mirrored radii.
short: Palindrome radii inside a known palindrome mirror each other.
long: Palindrome radii inside a known palindrome mirror each other. Separator characters unify even- and odd-length palindromes.
proof: Each centre's radius expands only beyond the current rightmost palindrome boundary, so total expansions are linear.
consequence: It is the optimal algorithm for longest-palindrome queries.

title: Rope Balanced Tree for Strings
subject: String Algorithms
statement: A rope represents a string as a balanced binary tree whose leaves hold short substrings, supporting concatenation and splitting in O(log n) time.
short: Avoid copying long strings when editing.
long: Avoid copying long strings when editing. Profitable weight balancing keeps tree height logarithmic after updates.
proof: Concatenation creates a new root; splitting follows one path and rebalances the two resulting trees.
consequence: Ropes are used in text editors and persistent string libraries.
